speechtext:
That the House resolve itself into committee on the following resolution :
That it is expedient to provide that pensions or gratuities may be granted to staff officers and officers and men of the permanent militia force, and to the widows and children of such officers, as follows :-
To an officer compulsorily retired, for any cause other than misconduct or inefficiency, after twenty years' service, or retiring voluntarily after thirty-five years' service, a pension not exceeding one-fiftieth of the pay and allowances of his rank or appointment at the time of his retirement for each year of service; service beyond thirty-five years not being reckoned.
To an officer who retires voluntarily after twenty-five years, but less than thirty-five years' service, a pension 20 per cent less than is above provided for.
Towards making good the said pensions, 5 per cent to be deducted from the pay of officers.
To an officer retiring on account of infirmity, or reltlred ito promote efficiency or economy in the service, a gratuity not exceeding one month's pay for each year's service; if retiring on account of injury received in the discharge of his duties, a gratuity not exceeding three months' pay for every two years' service. b To a non-commissioned officer or militiaman, if he has served fifteen but less than twenty-one years, a pension equal to one-fiftieth of his annual pay for every year of service; for twenty-one and less than twenty-five years service, twenty-fiftieths, and in addition two-fiftieths for every year over twenty; for twenty-five years, thirty-fiftieths, and in addition one-fiftieth for every year over twenty-five ; not exceeding, however, two-thirds of his average annual pay exclusive of extra pay or allowances
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE (Hon. F. W. Borden) moved :

speechtext:
during the three years preceding his retirement.	,	_	.
To the widow and children of an officer who had served twenty years and was at the time of his death on full pay or in receipt of pension, the following pension or allowance : in the ease of a colonel, $500 to the widow and $80 to each child; lieutenant-colonel, a pension of $450 to a widow and a yearly allowance of $80 to each child; major, $350 to widow and $70 to each child; captain, $250 to widow and $o5 to each child; lieutenant or second lieutenant, $200 to widow and $50 to each child; warrant officer, $100 to widow and $25 to each child ; the amount to children to be doubled if tbey are motherless and in need; no allowance to be granted to a son aged eighteen or a daughter aged twenty-one; and the total amount granted to the family of an officer in one year not to exceed the amount of the pension attached to his rank.
He said : Mr. Speaker, perhaps it would be more convenient to make the explanation in reference to this resolution before going into committee, and I will, therefore, detain the House a few minutes while I do so. The resolution proposes, for the first time in Canada, to adopt the principle of pensions for the permanent force of this country. Let me, at the outset, explain that the resolution, or the Act to be founded upon it, only applies to the permanent force and to the permanent staff, not to the active militia in the ordinary sense of the word. I make this statement as I think there has been some misapprehension abroad with reference to it. I do not think, in view of what appeared to be the general feeling of the House, evinced on a recent occasion, when a similar discussion was brought up by my hon. friend from Victoria, B.C. (Hon. Mr. Prior), that there is any need of my delaying the House to argue as to the advisability, the necessity and justice of adopting the pension system for our permanent corps. I may, however, say, in passing, that in every country, as far as I know, which has men permanently employed in the defence of the country, there is a pension system, and although we are only adopting it very late in the day, I believe it is a sound principle, which the country at large will approve.
Hear, hear.

There are special reasons, too, why, I think, the pension system should be adopted for our permanent force which are stronger even than in the case of ordinary soldiers. As I have frequently pointed out to the House, the permanent force of Canada is not simply a force organized as a nucleus to the army for defensive purposes. but is the educating force, it is the military school which supplies the teaching of the active militia of the country, and, therefore, while it is important- that we should have in the permanent force the very best class of men which can be obtained, it is important, having secured them, that

we should retain them. One of our difficulties has been to retain good men ; the very great difficulty which affects the non-commissioned officers and men is that they are poorly paid, and not taken care of when they get old, and, therefore, they are not inclined to remain except temporarily in the force. It is of the utmost importance, in order that this force should fully carry out what is expected of it, that permanency should he one of its characteristics. Now we come to the provisions contained in the resolution itself. It is divided, I may say, into two parts, and, first, I will refer to that part of the Bill which I am to introduce which provides for a pension to the non-commissioned [DOT]officers and men. I may say, in regard to this, that we have simply adopted the pension law of the North-west mounted police, which has been in operation since, I think, the year 1889. As indicating what the charge will be upon the country resulting from the adoption of this law, I may say that the North-west Mounted Police Pension Act. although enacted in 18S9, has practically been in force for twenty-eight years, namely, from the date at which the police force was organized, and at this moment the only charge entailed upon the country as a result of the operation of that pension law is the sum of $1,800 a year. The police force has numbered during most of these years about as many ns the permanent force ; somewhere about 1,000- sometimes below, and, I think, sometimes above that number-and, as I say, the only charge in which the country is involved as a result of the operation of the North-west Mounted Police Pension Act is to-day only $1,800 a year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Do we take a percentage from their pay ?

No. I may explain that under this Bill it is not intended to take any percentage from the pay of the non-commissioned officers and men. There is no deduction from the pay of the North-west mounted police, and the pay of these soldiers is so small that I think it would not be fair to ask privates and non-commissioned officers to contribute in that way. Now, it has seemed to me that there could be no possible reason which moved parliament to grant a pension to the North-west mounted police force, which does not apply equally to the permanent force of this country. That being the case, if there were no stronger reasons, it seems to me that it is a simple act of justice to apply the same law to the permanent force as has been applied to the North-west mounted police. I have just pointed out that our doing so will entail upon the country only a very moderate expense indeed. In this connection, I will repeat what I said a moment ago : That it is important to the success of
the work of the permanent force, that there should be permanency. We have got to do one thing or the other; we have either got to give these men much larger pay than they receive now, or else we must do without good men. I think it would be better to give this pension rather than increase the pay. The men who have served for many years become old, and have found it absolutely impossible, because of the low pay they'received to save anything, so that they are turned out on the world late in life to earn their living without anything in hand. The Militia Department is asked every year to give employment to some of these men, and that we do as well as we can, but how much better it would be to provide a pension by which, when these men have served their full term, they will be able to have something to live upon during the declining years of their life. I may point out in this connection that they must serve twenty years before they are entitled to a pension, or if through any disability they are unable to serve twenty years, then after fifteen years they will receive a pension. The pension is one-fiftieth of their pay for every year they have served up to two-thirds of their total pay ; that is the maximum they can receive under this law.
Now, Mr. Speaker, with reference to the other branch of this resolution which refers to officers, I desire to make this explanation. It has been said that this would involve a very serious charge upon the treasury. I am able to say that this is absolutely not the case. There will be no increased charge upon the treasury whatever, and I will point out how. At the present moment under the existing law, or under the existing order in council by which officers are retired from the service, any officer who has reached the age limit or is obliged to retire for other cause, receives on retirement, one-tenth of his pay for every year that he has served. To illustrate, suppose an officer has served twenty years, and suppose his pay was $2,000 a year, on retirement that officer would receive a gratuity equal to two years pay which would be $4,000. Without any desire to reflect upon the prudence of officers, I am bound to say that the experience of the department in reference to this method of treating them has been very unfortunate. We have had cases where officers have retired and have drawn large sums of money-some as high as $7,000 or $8,000-but from the very fact of their having lived for years without any experience in business, they have not been able to make the best use of the gratuity paid them. We find them coming back after a few years, perhaps after a few months, asking the Department of Militia, and asking the government to give them something to do, because they are again absolutely without means. I will not refer to anv cases by name, but I may say that

there are painful cases of this kind where officers who have commanded districts in this country are to-day asking us to give
them,	and are glad to get SI.25 a day to keep body and soul together, by taking care of a drill hall or doing some menial service of that kind. Now, that is not creditable to the country.
I propose then that this money which we have been paying under the order in council shall still be paid, but that it shall be paid in the form of an annuity. In other words, with that 10 per cent, for each year that the officer has served, instead of a gratuity, we shall buy for that officer an annuity. Well, Mr. Speaker, this would not be sufficient, and so I have decided to ask the officers themselves to contribute over and above this amount, a sufficient sum to give them a respectable retiring annuity. I may say that the amount which I am changing into the form of an annuity; the amount which we have been in the habit of giving for many years past would be enough to purchase one-half of a sufficient annuity. I have, after consulting on the matter with the superintendent of insurance, ascertained that a tax of 5 per cent upon the pay of the officers, added to that which they are already entitled to. and put into the consolidated fund, would at the rate of 34 per cent-I may say that the interest lias been computed at that low rate in all these calculations-at the rate of 3| per cent it would secure for these officers the pension which is mentioned in the resolution, and which I intend to incorporate in the Bill. I think,
then.	I have demonstrated that the proposal which I bring before the House, so far as the officers are concerned, does not involve an additional dollar of expense or taxation on the people of this country ; and therefore, although I would have been prepared to go further, I think no one in this House can object to the proposal.
The Bill which I intend to found on these resolutions has been drawn from several sources. The old Civil Service Superannuation Act has been used as a basis for that portion of the Bill which applies to tlie officers. I have already explained that that portion which applies to non-commissioned officers and men is a literal copy of the North-west Mounted Police Pension Act, which has been in force since 1889. That portion which applies to officers' wives and children is taken from the Royal Warrant for pay. The rate which we ask the officers to contribute, namely, 5 per cent, is a large rate, much larger than the civil service were asked to contribute under the old Civil1 Service Superannuation Act. But we had in view the fact that we intended to give not only officers but officers' wives the benefit of this law. and we felt that the officers, in view of that fact, would be willing to contribute the o per cent which we ask of them.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: In conclusion, I have only to repeat what I said in opening, that I am confident that we are only dioing a simple act of justice, which ought to have been done long ago, and at the same time we are taking the very best means we could possibly take to ensure to this country a vast improvement in our permanent force; and. the money which we shall expend in this way will be trifling compared with the immense advantage to the country, because it will result in greater advantage from the expenditure which we are making annually not only on the permanent force, but on the active militia of the country. I have much pleasure in moving the House into committee on the resolution.

So far as the proposals go, I think they will meet with the very j cordial approval of the members of this ! House. I would like, however, to call the minister's attention to the fact that as the resolutions read, they do not provide for those officers who have been retired-men who have been brigade majors, or who have occupied other high positions in the | service, and have been retired by the gov-| eminent when they have reached the age limit of sixty years or for some other reason. I would like to know whether the ; minister proposes in any way to provide for them.
The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DE-[ FENCE. Those officers come under the I class to which I referred as having already j received the gratuity ; and, unless we make some special provision for them, they could | not be very well included, because they are | no longer in either of the classes referred ! to in the resolution, and have already been Paid the money to which they were entitled under the system which has been in force for a great many years.

Even so, the minister knows very well-because he has just told us that the gratuity they received has long since been spent, and that these men are to-day in necessitous circumstances; and I think it would be a reflection on this country if these men, who have devoted the best years of their lives to the service of their country at a small remuneration, were left in that position. I am told that there are about a dozen officers who would be thus included in the list. They have an equally strong claim with those "whom the minister proposes to provide for, and I would ask him to consider carefully their case. I do not suggest that the pension be made retroactive, because the gratuity which they receive, we will say. will do them up to the present time, but that it be made to date from the present time. I think the government could do no more meritorious act than to include these men in the prolusion they are making.

Mr. Speaker, I may be allowed one or two words in reply to the hon. minister, in order to congratulate him on at last having brought down this most meritorious measure. I suppose that when the Bill comes before the House we shall have a better chance of discussing- the different clauses in it; but I would like to draw the hon. minister's attention to one or two matters. He has informed the House that it is not intended that the non-commissioned officers and men of the permanent corps should be called upon to contribute to any superannuation fund. I would ask him whether the officers of the Northwest mounted police pay anytning to the fund ?
The officers of the North-west mounted police are urder the Civil Service Superannuation Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: What percentage do they pay ?

It was 3i per cent; but my hon. friend will remember that the Superannuation Act was repealed, and to-day they are paying 5 per cent, just as the civil servants are, which they receive back with interest as a gratuity.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Well, it seems to me it is acting on a wrong principle to ask these officers to contribute anything. As the hon. gentleman says, the amount charged to the country for the pension fund of the non-commissioned officers and men of the North-west mounted police is the insignificant sum of $1,800 a year. It seems to me that Canada can well afford to stand any little expense which this pension Bill would entail upon the treasury. The number of men is very small, and even if they were asked to contribute anything the amount would be very little. It seems to me rather hard that officers in Canada should be asked to contribute to a fund of this kind when no other officers in the same positions, in any other part of the world, are called upon to do so. However, I suppose half a loaf is better than no bread. But I do hope that before this Bill passes, hon. gentlemen on both sides will see that it would be more creditable to Canada to have the clause struck out and a pension given, without asking either the officers or men to contribute anything.

I would like to ask the minister for some information. I am not sure whether the hon. member for West York asked it or not, but if so, I did not catch the reply. I have received a communication from a gentleman who is a retired staff officer, and who says :
There are about a dozen retired staff officers now earning a precarious living the best way
possible in order to keep themselves out of the poorhouse.
And he wants to know whether it is intended in any way to consider the position of these gentlemen and include them in the gratuities proposed to be given.
I have also received a communication from an old friend of mine, who was in the militia force nearly thirty years, but has since been discharged. He gives me a record of the service he has done. He was in the Queen's Own, in the first and second Red river expeditions, in the North-west expedition of 1885, and in the permanent corp-And he asks, is it possible that men who have rendered services, as he has, extending over twenty-five or thirty years, but who are not now in the force, can come under this provision ?
I have another question to ask. There is this paragraph in the resolution :
To an officer who retired voluntarily after twenty-five years', but less than thirty-five years', service, a pension 20 per cent less than is above provided for.
Is it intended that officers who will come under the provisions of this resolution four or five years from now, will have a deduction made from their pension by reason of the fact that they will only have contributed this 5 per cent for a very short period ?

The hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace) did inquire with reference to the first matter raised by my hon. friend and I replied that the officers referred to had already beeu provided for, so far as we were able, under existing regulations. That is to say, they had received their retiring gratuity of 10 per cenr of their pay for each year's service. I agree with the hon. member for West York that there are cases of extreme hardship which ought to be looked into, but I do not know whether such eases can be met in connection with this Bill. I have my doubts on that point, but I do think that special cases might be dealt with in a special way by a special proposal to parliament, and I will be prepared to look into that matter and make a proposal later on, if thought advisable.
With reference to the last question, which the hon. member for Toronto has put, regarding these officers who have paid into the fund for a year or two, or who have not paid at all, I may say that all officers will come under the operation of this Act the day it becomes law, and there is a provision by which, when a pension is paid there shall be a deduction made of 5 per cent from the pension payable, for the number of years those officers have not paid.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I think the hon. minister deserves a great deal of credit for the manner in which he has shown his interest

in this particular service. The resolution is worthy of support. I wish the House to understand that while I am opposed to pensions and superannuations and that sort of thing, I think that this can he made an exception. Those who are to benefit are a class of people who receive very inadequate pay for the services they render, and who, therefore, are entitled to recognition in the way provided by this resolution. I do not believe that the expenditure will be at all serious, because there will be a call on the salaries of the officers each year of 5 per cent, and that will probably meet the calls to be made on the government for pensions or come very near meeting tjiem. Therefore, I have no hesitation in supporting the resolution most heartily, being convinced that it is in the interests of the country.
Are the permanent corps mentioned as such in the Militia Act or included just in the ordinary active militia ?

They are not mentioned in the Militia Act by that name. There is a provision in the Militia Act for the enrolling of 1,000 men for special service, but they are not called a permanent force. We have made that sufficiently clear in the Bill to cover any difficulties. The first clause fully sets out what the different names indicate.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The pensions or gratuities are to be given to widows and children. I would like to have a definition of the term 'children.'
The Bill provides for all these details. I think the age is eighteen for a boy and twenty-one for a girl.
speakername: Tiie MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Before the House went into committee, I asked two or three questions of the hon. minister. He answered all but one of them-that with reference to non-commissioned officers and men who have served for many years, but are not now in active service. Is it possible in any way to have these men come under the provisions of this Act ?

When we come to consider the Bill, possibly something may be done, although, as I said in the case of the retired staff officers, it would probably be better to deal with such men as special eases. This Act will not cover such cases unless the men are now in the permanent force, either in connection with the stores or in some active branch of the permanent force.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Will there be provision in the Bill authorizing the minister to deal with these special cases ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Then, how can they be dealt with ?
What I meant was that when we came to the consideration of the Bill, perhaps some amendment might be proposed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Are these pensions proportioned to the pay of officers ?	*
Xes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I understand this pension scheme is based on the pension scheme of the North-west mounted police ?
Yes, for non-commissioned officers and men.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I wish to point out what I consider a very serious flaw in the Northwest mounted police scheme. I would mention one particular case, that of Major Belcher, second in command of the Strathcona Horse. He served in the mounted police-

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) will excuse me, but the officers do not come under the Act that I have copied, but under the old civil service superannuation system. Consequently, remarks relating to the officers of the North-west mounted police do not apply in this case.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I do not know whether we understand each other. Suppose a non-commissioned officer receives a commission, he stands to receive a pension counted only from the date of his commission. In the case of Major Belcher lie served for some twenty odd years as private and non-commissioned officer, and that period of his service is left out of consideration when his pension is counted.

I am happy to be able to tell my hon. friend that we have improved on the North-west mounted police in that respect. We now allow privates or non-commissioned officers who become officers to count the time during which they served in the ranks or as non-commissioned officers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Supposing a man served ten years as a non-commissioned officer and ten years as an officer, would that count as ten years as officer at the same rank as at retirement ?

Yes.
Resolution reported.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
Bill (No. 121) further to amend the Post Office Act (Hon. Mr. Sutherland), was read the second time, and considered in committee.
On section 1,

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What is the change affected by this amendment ?
Hon. ill'. SUTHERLAND. The only change is in the fourth line of the subsection following the words ' Postmaster General,' where the words ' whether such letter is addressed to a real or fictitious person or not,' are inserted. The [DOT] Bill was drafted by the Justice Department, and, comparing it with the Act, I 'notice that there seems to be some little change in the wording, but the changes do not affect the law except in the words I have quoted. In many cases the officers of the department render services in prosecutions for stealing registered letters and other misconduct ; and the question has been raised whether a post letter addressed to a fictitious person came under the Act. In a recent case in Quebec a convict is now serving a five years term in the penitentiary for stealing a letter, and this question was raised, and the judge in that case held-I think it was on appeal- that the interpretation we put upon it did apply to a fictitious person. We think it well to make it clear, because in many cases this point is being raised by the lawyers defending accused persons.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is to say, the point has arisen in cases where letters have been posted for the purpose of securing evidence against a party suspected of having purloined a letter ?

It is not so much for the purpose" of getting evidence, as of finding out who are the thieves, and of pursuing the course of the missing registered letter.
On section 2,

This is taking power to establish dead letter offices in the places mentioned in addition to those now having dead letter offices, namely, Montreal, Toronto, Victoria, Winnipeg, Halifax and Ottawa. We are taking power to establish, in addition, dead letter offices at St. John, Kingston, Hamilton, London, Vancouver and Dawson. I understand from the officers of the department that this system has worked very satisfactorily. It is being used now at some of these points with regard to newspapers, and it is found desirable to extend the system to the places named.

Is it intended that these new dead letter offices shall be under the charge of the local officers, or will it be necessary to appoint new officers at these places ?
Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND^ I do not think it will be necessary to increase tne staff. The same staff, probably, will do the work.
On section 3,

This section gives the department power to make a contract for eight years, instead of four, for the carriage of mails. It has been found in many cases that the department could make a saving by making contracts for longer terms.

Would not that rule work both ways ? It might be found that you could make a more favourable contract for a shorter term ; for instance, at the end of four years you might be able to make a better contract than you did in the beginning of the four years term.

Of course, the department retains discretion to make the contract for the longer term. It is true this xirovision might work the other way, in some cases; but, we find at the present time that money would be saved by making the contracts for a longer term, there is no doubt about that. Any hon. gentleman can see that when a contractor has to provide one or more horses and vehicles to carry out a contract, the longer the term is the cheaper he is willing to take the contract for. If the term is short, he knows that it may not be renewed to him. and that if somebody else puts in a lower tender, he is likely to lose the contract, and to suffer loss on his investment in horses and vehicles, and so forth. But this is a discretionary power, and it would not always be wise to exercise it.
Is the change being made on the advice of the executive officers of the Post Office Department ?
Exclusively on their advice. This whole Bill was prepared by the department, and I am advised by the officers that it is desirable in the interest of economy.

I think the minister had better stick to the old law. This amendment gives power to the department to renew contracts without competition for eight years instead of four. Power of renewal after four years was enough.
For any amount ?

For any amount. For instance, $30,000 is now being paid on a contract for carrying mails to Kamloops, and there are some other large contracts in the North-west Territories. Parties may then come to the department and get a renewal for eight years without any competition I think the hon. gentleman has sufficient power already in letting contracts for four years.
4243

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: The old rule before the present government came into power was, I think, that a contract for $200 or less might be renewed for another four years, if performed satisfactorily. That is the system that now obtains throughout the country.
I understood the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) to say that under the old law you could renew for any amount.
I think so.

I am basing my statement upon information which I repeatedly heard from the Postmaster General, that if a contract was for $200 or under it might be renewed ; but if it was more than $200, it must be put up to tender again. But it came out that many contracts had been renewed that were over $200. The present Postmaster General took great credit to himself for having cancelled a number of contracts and relet them after advertisement, and he contended that a great saving had been effected by that system ; but, when supporting it by argument, he contended that the principle of renewing contracts was wrong, and, therefore, he had not followed it. What I want to draw attention to is the fact that the very same system is being followed to-day by the Postmaster General which he condemned in unstinted language only a few years ago. I do not want to be understood as condemning the system, because I have always thought that if the work was being satisfactorily performed at a reasonable price, it was a proper thing to renew the contract. But I find that the Postmaster General has now fallen into the old practice which he so vigorously condemned under his predecessor.
Now, he proposes to go very much farther, and without even inquiring as to how the work is being done from the beginning, to make a cpntract for eight years instead of four. I am not saying that it will be bad, or that it will be good, but I am inclined to think, that, in some respects, it would turn out badly because there is sometimes the habit amongst those who propose to send in tenders to come to an understanding between each other as to their tenders. Of course, X presume that under such circumstances, or in any circumstances, the department would still have the right to, at any time, cancel any of these contracts when it is shown that in the public interest, they should be cancelled and tenders invited again. I do not know whether this new system will be good or bad. It does not seem to me that the hon. acting minister has given us reasons sufficient to justify him in departing from the well understood principle that we followed so long. These reasons are quite insufficient to justify such a radical departure. If it was proposed to Mr. HAGGART.
extend the time from four years to six, rather than from four years to eight, I would think that it might be a move in the right direction.

I think the proposal to substitute the word ' eight ' for the word ' four ' is utterly unjustifiable. The hon. minister's statement to us was that this was something recommended by the officers of his department. Well, he has*, given no reason, as I understood him, except that.
Yes, I did.
The officers of his department may be quite willing to have a contract renewed for twenty years, so that they may be saved from any further trouble.
I gave another reason beside that.

The very thing that the hon. Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock) has staked his existence upon and boasted of all through the country, is that he has cancelled contracts that were renewed without tender, and that he has thereby saved large sums of money to the country. What are we to say now ? He has got the contracts and he proposes not to renew them for four years, but to do that which has never been done before-to renew them for eight years. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) raises the question whether this word ' eight ' refers to the first letting of the contract, or to renewing it. Which is it ?
To the first letting only.
What about the renewal ? When this renewal takes place, after another eight years, is it again renewed ?
That is rather a technical point. I will look into it.
That is vital to the Bill.

I will look into it, and see whether that will be the result of this amendment or not. It was not brought to my attention. I do not think that would be the effect. I think it says in the Act how long the renewal is for.
But the hon. minister is not able to say ?
I would not like to be certain about it. This is a legal point.

I presume that when a contract is let for eight years in the first instance the renewal will be for the same length of time. I am quite opposed to the' principle altogether. There is no reason why such should be done. It will practically mean that a person getting a contract will have it for sixteen years if the renewal
*

is for the same time. If the renewal he not for the same time, then it would be for twelve years at any rate. There is no doubt about that. Let us consider what would be the effect in the case of large contracts. There is a large contract on the Cariboo road from Ashcroft, B.C., northward. That contract was taken from the old contractors, tenders were submitted by certain gentlemen, and they are carrying it out. They can have it for twelve years at any rate without new tenders being invited.
Eight years.

The Post Office Act says:
No contract shall be entered into for a longer term than four years, hut the Postmaster General may, In special cases, when, in his opinion, the service has been satisfactorily performed under an expiring contract, and on conditions advantageous to the public interest, renew the same with the same contractor for a further term not exceeding four years.
There is no limitation as to the amount to be paid. The Bill says :
Subsection 2 of section 61 of the Post Office Act is amended by the substitution of the word 'eight' for the word 'four' in the second line and in the sixth line of the said subsection.
The hon. acting Postmaster General was not quite sure. From what I have read he is quite sure. From that it can be renewed for eight years. The Act says, in the second line, ' four years,' but under this amendment it will read that:
No contract shall be entered into for a longer term than eight years.
The sixth line of the Act says that the Postmaster General may renew the contract for a further term not exceeding four years, but, by the amendment, the ' four ' is converted into an ' eight,' so that the renewal will be for eight years, and therefore, it is for sixteen years.

1 can quite readily see that there are two sides to this question. There are no doubt many cases coming under the notice of the officers of the department in which they think it will be an advantage to make contracts for a longer time. I do not feel desirous of pressing the matter. I have no doubt that it might work out both ways. I would move that the clause be struck out.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

I do not think that it makes very much difference whether it is four years or eight years with the present government. My own experience in Prince Edward Island is that I find that they cancel contracts which were entered into in good faith and give them to their friends. Now, what do they propose to do by this Bill ? They propose to appoint, under this government, a staff of practically permanent men for a term of eight years. Four years is long enough.
That clause has been struck out.

I asked the acting Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Sutherland), a few days ago, a question in connection with the carrying of the mails in Prince Edward Island. This is only a small contract, but it is the principle that we object to. The old contractor, Mr. ICehoe, happened to be a Conservative. He had been carrying the mails for four years with great acceptance, and performing his contract in good faith. He was requested by the post office inspector at Charlottetown, when the term had expired, to enter into an agreement for the next four years. He did that, and he also signed a bond. I know that he signed the bond, because I witnessed it. Acting in good faith with the government, having carried the mails for four years, and having signed a bond for four years more, he believed that he would be fully entitled to his rights under the contract. In a month or j so afterwards the Post Office Department cancelled that bond, and without inviting tenders, gave the contract to a friend of theirs, and gave him $15 a year more for the same work. The hon. acting Postmaster General shakes his head. He told me the other day, and I have it under my hand now, that the present contractor is receiving $15 a year more for carrying these mails than Mr. Kehoe did it for. How are you going to compensate Mr. Kehoe, who after having used his horses and his carriages and his harness and other appliances for these four years, believed he was entering into a contract with the government of Canada for four years more, and renewed a large part of these appliances. For mere party purposes you ruthlessly take away from him the rights he acquired under contract, and you give them to a follower of your own at a cost of $15 a year more for doing the same work. That is the way you are treating the people of Canada. This particular contract is a small one, but if you take $15 a year in connection with all the post offices over Canada, you will be wasting thousands and thousands of dollars of the money of the people. Without inviting public tenders, and after Mr. Kehoe had signed his bonds giving good security to go on with this business for four years, then for the sake of helping a party follower, you do Mr. Kehoe a great wrong. It is an outrage and a shame.
Section withdrawn.
On section 4,

A number of these contracts have been cancelled by the department without assigning any reason whatever, and the Minister of Justice has refused the parties a fiat to bring their cases before the court. I always understood that the Act giving the Crown power to grant a fiat was virtually self-acting. Applica-

tions have been made in dozens of these cases where the contract has been cancelled, and the government have refused a flat to these parties who claimed that they have suffered damages. On -what grounds, I ask the minister, have these fiats been refused 1

I must say that no such case has come under my notice since I have been in the department. My hon. friend must have been misinformed when he says that such cases exist. As to the clause which has just been dropped, I may say that, judging from the remarks of the hon. member for Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hackett) and the ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Haggart), it would seem that probably we had better be guided by the judgment of the officers of the department than by discussion here. It would appear from their observations that there are good reasons why it should be left to the discretion of the department as to the period for which a contract might be made. If that were the case, the grievances which the hon. gentleman says exist in his district probably would not exist. I shall make inquiries in the department about the matter to which the ex-Postmaster General has referred and give the information.
Can the minister tell the number of contracts cancelled each year during the last four or five years ?
That is not the point which my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) brought up, but I will be glad to get that information.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I may say that these petitions to which my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has referred, were mentioned in the House last year. I moved for a return of all the papers, and afterwards the matter was discussed. The petitions, as I understand, have been for about two years before the Postmaster General, for the purpose of having him transmit them with his report to the proper officer. There were at least twenty of them, if I remember aright, and the point raised was whether under the terms of the contracts the Crown had a legal right to terminate them. I looked at the contracts, and it seemed to me from a hasty examination of the question that it was a perfectly proper case to submit to the Exchequer Court. I do think that it is a public scandal that petitions of right should lie for a year and a half or two years, without having any action taken upon them or any report made by the Postmaster General with respect to them. If the Crown had no legal right to cancel these contracts and the Postmaster General was wrong in doing so, then the Crown should accept responsibility for that and these men should not be kept waiting without an answer. It is a matter which well deserves the attention of the acting Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Sutherland), and if the circumstances are Mr. HAGGART.
as I believe them to be, there should be no further delay whatever in giving these men a fiat if they ask for it.

The charge which the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Hackett) has made against the Postmaster General certainly should be inquired into, and if what the hon. gentleman states be true, then a great injustice has been done. I did not think it possible that the government could be guilty of anything of the kind.
You haven't got your eyeteeth cut yet.

If they are guilty they should make amends for it and see that it does not occur again. The idea of the Postmaster General cancelling the contract of a man who has given satisfaction for three or four years, without any other reason than that the contractor was not a party politician, is a disgrace to Canada. I do not think that the acting Postmaster General can be accused of this, because he has only taken the portfolio for a short time, but I hope he will inquire into it and never let the thing occur again.
Hear, hear.

Considering the number of grievances we hear from Prince Edward Island, it would appear that that island must be very badly governed. One day the grievance is against the Minister of Marine, next day against the Minister of Railways, next against the Postmaster General, and probably four or five days of the session have been devoted to Prince Edward Island. In the future, it would be better for us to set apart two or three days each session for the purpose of hearing the grievances of that island. I am happy to say that I belong to an island that is represented by as many members as come from ' the Island,' and that we have no grievances at all, so that in that respect we differ from Prince Edward Island. Now, where there are large contracts involving a large amount of money there is very keen competition, and very often the contractors take the work at a rather low price. In that case they fit themselves with carriages, horses, and drivers, and establish stations at different places ; and if the time were extended for four years longer they would have an opportunity, perhaps, of recouping themselves for some of the expenses they Incurred in the preparation. That is all I want to say on that subject, and I have my doubts about the government considering all the grievances which we hear from Prince Edward Island.

I have listened with some pleasure to the rebuke which has been administered to me by the hon. member for Victoria, Cape .Breton. He is almost paternal in this House, having been a mem-

ber of a former government; but I am here representing an intelligent body of people, and it is my right on the floor of parliament to advocate what is in the interests of the people of Canada. The hon. gentleman may sit down and imagine that he is beside the Bras d'Or Lakes; but he cannot say that a man who rises in this House and shows where the government are taking the money of this country and giving it to their favourites, is not doing right. I have shown, and the acting Postmaster General has not been able to refute it, that this small contract, amounting to $35 a year, was taken from a man who had entered into a bond to carry it four years longer, was cancelled and given to a favourite of the government at an advance of 40 per cent. Am I to be told by the hon. member for Victoria that I am to sit quietly and allow such an outrage to be committed on the people ? I admire the venerable gentleman, and the position he has held in the past, but he is not going to rebuke me or dictate what I am to do here as a representative of the people having equal rights with him. Mr. Kehoe, having carried the mails for four years to the satisfaction of the people, was asked by the post office inspector of Prince Edward Island if he would renew his contract for four years longer. He replied in the affirmative. A bond was sent to him; I witnessed it as a justice of the peace and saw it signed by two sureties for the sum of $35 a year for carrying the mails. A month afterwards or thereabouts the Postmaster General cancelled that contract and gave it to a friend of his own for $50 a year. Although the amount is small, it is the underlying principle of good faith on the part of the people of Canada that is important. If you do the same thing all over Canada, what is going to become of the people of Canada ? Where is this reckless extravagance, this corruption, this taking of the people's money for the purpose of gaining political support, going to end ? Sir, we want honest government in this country; we want justice and fair-play; and we are here, my hon. friend from Victoria, venerable as he is, and old as I am myself, to look after the interests of the people. We are veterans; we have fought our battles in the past in the interests of the country; but, Sir, I am not going to be admonished by him. I am his equal in every respect-at least, I feel that I am-and I am not going to have this rebuke administered to me on the floor of this House without resenting it.

I am not going to reply to my hon. friend. I merely wish to say that I have not lived on the Bras d'Or Lake, but in the city of Halifax, for the last twenty-seven years; so that he is altogether mistaken as to my place of residence. The only other remark I intend to make is that I think there is no other man in this House who has occupied half the time that
has been occupied by the hon. gentleman who has just sat down. There has not been a week since we came to this parliament in which he has not had a new grievance. I begin to think that the government is all right or that he is all wrong-either one or the other.

1 know that the hon. gentleman does not desire to have the time of the House taken up in these discussions; but we are here for that purpose. What do the people send the members here for, but to discuss the affairs of the country ? The hon. gentleman may feel very secure; he would like to go back and draw his pension of $800 a year from the government. He may feel that he has nothing to do with the interests of his constituents, but they will hold him responsible for his conduct here. I tell you, Prince Edward Island, small as it is, is composed of an intelligent population; and although there are only two of us here from that pi'o-vince, we will take no back seats; and if the hon. gentleman thinks he is doing justice to his constituents by getting up here and interrupting me, he is very much mistaken.
All I can say to the hon. gentleman is that if he is as safe before his constituents as I am before mine, he will come back here at the next general election.

The hon.
gentleman has stated that this contract was renewed and cancelled. I, of course, cannot make a definite statement, because I have no information in regard to it. All I can say is that I will inquire. I have very grave doubts that the Postmaster General or the department would cancel any contract that had been made. One cannot help but feel that the credit of the country is pledged when a contract is signed, and it would only be for very good cause indeed, such as neglect of duty in carrying out the contract in some material way, that any such cancellation would take place. However, I will make inquiries as to what did take place.
Will the acting Postmaster General promise that when he gets that information he will bring it down to the House ?
Certainly. I do not think it would be the policy of the Postmaster General or the department to do any such thing.

I take this opportunity to bring to the notice of the acting Postmaster General a case in the county of Pictou which is a rather singular one, in which a contract which expired about the 1st of March has not been relet at all. It may be that the work of advertising and scanning the tenders is too severe for the

*department, or tliere may be some other reason why they do not care to renew the contract. It was taken at an exceedingly low price by the contractor who held it previously, and when it expired it was not advertised.
Does the bon. member remember the name ?

It was a contract for carrying- the mails from a station to River John and from River Joan to Hedge-ville-a double contract. When the contract expired, it was transferred to another Individual without tender at all, but the price was so exceedingly low that the new contractor has not accepted the contract, and for some months that very extraordinary state of affairs exists, that a contract is so favourable to the department that no other person can be got to take it at the same figure, and It is in abeyance. Possibly the reason why the hon. minister now wishes to let contracts for eight years, is to avoid the difficulty, labour and trouble involved in releting them. But I think really such an extraordinary case as this should receive the attention of the department. I brought this matter to the notice of the government some months ago, and no action has yet been taken.

In the Post Office Department many cases arise in which there is necessarily delay. Probably the one referred to is one that was brought to my attention a few days ago, in which the lowest tenderer was reported by the inspector as not being able to procure bonds.
No.

There are several cases of that kind. When advertisements are published, low tenders are often put in by parties who are unable to furnish bonds. On the whole, I believe, after hearing the discussion here, we probably made a mistake in striking this out. It would no doubt avoid a great deal of expense if many of these contracts, which are let to responsible men at low figures, were made for longer terms. I have not interfered in any way with the conduct of affairs by the officials of the department, but in many cases we have to take the next lowest tenderer, if he is at all satisfactory and responsible.

In this case, although the contract had expired, tenders were not called for, and the contract was given to a friend of the government without tenders, but the price was so low that the friends of the government would not take it. I am sure that the acting minister will see the necessity of doing something in this matter. He would be perfectly justified in giving the contract without tender for an additional term of four years to the original contractor,1 who was the best man in the neighbourhood, who can secure bonds to any amount, Mr. BELL (Pictou).
and who took the work at so low a price that it cannot be let to any one else at the same figure.
If the hon. gentleman will send me a note, I will see what I can do in the matter.

I wish to call attention to a similar case in West York and ask the hon. minister to give it the same attention. I refer to the contract for carrying the mails to Carrville and Sherwood. I will give the hon. minister a memo, and will expect the information to be brought down. My information is that tenders were called for, that the lowest tender was not accepted, and a higher rate paid another party, although the lowest tenderer had given ample security and was thoroughly responsible.
Mr. KADLnACH. I wish to draw attention to a ease in my county similar to that mentioned by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell). A contract was entered into by a party some years ago. It expired and tenders were called for and submitted to the department. How many I do not know, but I know of two that were submitted. The party who made the lowest tender, though not a friend of mine politically, was instructed to enter on the work at once, as the lowest tenderer, which he did, and carried the mails for some short time. The service was from my own town to the railway station. After having performed the service a few days, it is supposed that remonstrances were made to the department for having given this contract to the lowest tenderer, and lie got notice that he was recalled, and his services not required. The other party, whose tender was higher, is now doing the work.
I would like to- know why such a course was adopted. If there is any principle in such matters, I want to see it carried out. I wish the hon. minister to understand that the party who is now doing the work, and who was the highest tenderer, is a friend of mine, whereas the party who was the lowest tenderer and from whom the work was taken, after it had been given to him, is not a friend of mine and never was. I am simply drawing attention to this in order that we may know whether the government is acting on anv principle, and if so that principle should be carried out strictly to the letter.
On section 4,
What are to be the duties of these porters ?

At present, in many cases, several days in the week, especially when the mails are leaving large cities, there is much more mail matter than the mail messenger can attend to, and an extra mail messenger has to be put on the ear. Under the law he is entitled to his mileage. We thought that a class of employees, styied

train porters, might do this work satisfactorily and a very considerable saving effected. That is the only object.
The porters do not get any mileage.

No, they have a fixed salary. As these porters will have to be competent officials and pass the civil service examination, I thought that after a certain service they should be entitled to promotion to the position of mail clerk. It is only proper to encourage young men by giving them some prospect of advancement.
Will they do exactly the same duties as the mail clerk ?

Hardly the same. The mail clerk is responsible for the distribution of the letters. When we have to send a railway messenger with the regular mail clerk, his principal duty is to handle the mail. He does not distribute letters, or make reports, but principally does manual labour. So that it is principally manual labour, the handling of parcels and bags. The only employee in the service for this purpose is a mail messenger, who receives a much larger salary than these men would, and also draws his mileage.
Will the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) kindly make inquiry of his officials with regard to the matter I have been complaining of-the mail service between Lunenburg and the railway station ?

If my hon. friend will be kind enough to give me a memorandum of the matter, I shall be glad to get the information for him. So far as I am concerned, and I am sure, so far as the department is concerned, the only anxiety is to get the best service at the most reasonable rate. It is foolish to think that we can distinguish, or ought to distinguish, between these various mail contractors and others politically, or in any such fashion. The hon. gentleman will find that these matters, as a rule, are left to the inspectors, and that their recommendations are usually carried out. It may be that the inspectors or officers have made mistakes, or have not used the best judgment. But, I think that, on the whole, the service has been very satisfactorily carried out. and without any particular political influence.
The hon. minister will see that I am not offering any undue criticism. The only thing is, that if the department is establishing a principle, I want to see that principle carried out to the letter.

How many of these railway porters will be required ? And how will they be provided for ? I suppose they will be provided for in the supplementary estimates, as I think there is no item in the main estimates.
The number will probably be four or five, perhaps half a dozen. Of course, a vote will be taken in the estimates to provide for them.
What pay do the men who transfer the mail to the station and handle bags at the post office receive now on entering the service ?
I think they are paid $400 a year.

I observe that subsection 2 of this section provides that appointees to this class must have passed the preliminary examination. Are appointments being made now to the post office service of persons who have not passed this examination ?
1 understand there are no appointments to the railway mail service-
But, I am speaking of porters and letter carriers-are they required to pass the preliminary examination ?
I believe so. They could not be retained in the service otherwise.

Evidently the aim is to promote these young men to be railway mail clerks, because it is provided that any train porter who has had three years' service as such and who has passed the qualifying civil service examination, and also such examination in duties as the Postmaster General prescribes, shall be eligible for appointment to the rank of railway mail clerk. I take it, that it is supposed that as railway porters they would be learning the business. So, I suppose, they will be expected to do a good deal more than the mere manual labour of handling the mail bags, for they could not learn much of the business if confined to that alone.

This amendment was made at my own suggestion, in looking over the Act with the officer. At present, if a young man has passed the qualification examination, he is made a mail clerk without any experience. Appointments to the position of train porters are confined to young men of from eighteen to twenty-four years of age. In such a position he would naturally gain some experience. If they have shown themselves steady and well qualified, and passed the qualifying examination, I thought it omy fair that they should not be debarred from receiving an appointment. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) will agree that that is quite right.

I am not raising any objection to it. I should think the service of train porter would be the best school in which to learn the duties of mail clerk. But, it seemed to me, that when the minister spoke of their work being merely that of

handling mail bags, that would be a poor introduction to the duties of the mail clerk.

A clever young man, who is associated with the mail clerk, would naturally be given wrork to do that would give him an opportunity to improve himself in the service. Such a man passing the qualifying examination would naturally prove himself a very good mail clerk indeed.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: A gentleman has telegraphed to me suggesting that instead of fixing the day on the 24th of May, it should be made the fourth Monday in May, so that it will always come on the same day of the week. I mention this for the consideration of the House.

If there is anything in the idea of making the holiday at all, we had better stick to the 24th.
Mr. BORDEN Halifax). I dare say that may be better. His idea was still to call it Victoria Day, but to have a particular Monday in May always observed.
On section 3,	.

speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
The PRIME MINISTER moved that subsection 2 of section 14 of the Bills of Exchange Act, 1900, is amended by adding to the days to be observed in the several provinces as legal holidays or non-juridical days, * Victoria Day.'

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The only objection to putting that amendment in this particular place is that it might be misleading to any one looking at the Bills of Exchange Act, unless there is something in the title of this Act to attract attention. Any person desiring, for the purpose of bills of exchange. to know what are legal holidays, might be misled.

1 doubt it, because the Act will be widely known as Victoria Day. I think the Act will have some publicity in that respect, and, moreover, we contemplate an early consolidation, including this statute.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That will answer the objection if, when that consolidation takes place, this will receive its proper place in that Act.
Is that the best designation that could be given to the day ? We have always called it Queen's Birthday.
The Queen's Birthday was the holiday according to the Interpretation Act. Now the birthday of the Sovereign is the 9th of November.
I meant whether Victoria Day is the best designation to be given to the holiday. What about Queen Victoria holiday ?
I think Victoria Day is quite enough, everybody will understand it.
We always knew it by the name of Queen's Birthday.

We do not generally keep a birthday after death.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W.
S.	Fielding). We could not adopt the phrase ' Queen's Birthday,' because that might be understood to be the birthday of Queen Alexandra. The expression would be misleading.
My hon. friend's proposition was to call it Queen Victoria Day.
She is not Queen now.
Is it proposed to have the celebration of Victoria Day take the place of the celebration of . the birthday of the Sovereign ?
No, it is an additional holiday.
If you are going to celebrate the birthday of the present Sovereign it will come very close to Thanksgiving Day.

I trust we are not laying the foundation for future efforts in this direction. There may be a time coming when we will have no day to work in.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

I would ask the permission of the minister to bring up a matter here in connection with the Cornwall canal, as I may not be present when that item is reached. In 1897 there was a gentleman named Timothy Shields, who had been in the employment of the government for a period of twenty-eight years. On the 12th of April he received a communication from the Department of Railways and Canals to the effect that his services were dispensed with, and on the 19th of April he made the usual application for superannuation, and in reply received a letter from the Department of Railways and Canals stating that the question of his superannuation allowance would come up for consideration at a later date. Subsequently he received a notice that he was deprived entirely of superannuation. He was at a loss to understand why that should be the case, he having served for twenty-eight years in the Department of Railways and Canals, and having contributed to the superannua-1344
I regret it as much as any one that you have not had your matter settled in some way. Not only your own matter, but several matters as well as yours, should have been settled on.
Then he winds up his letter by stating :
Mr. Scott and myself have been urging your matter, and have no intention of allowing the matter to drop.
When I was elected to represent Cornwall and Stormont, Mr. Shields, whom I have known for many years, came to me and stated his grievance. I then made inquiry from the department in the town of Cornwall at the head of the Cornwall canal, and I found that Mr. Shields was one of the best officials who had ever been connected with the Cornwall canal, and that he had always given entire satisfaction, and could not have been dismissed because he was not a thoroughly competent official. I found that subsequently, notwithstanding this letter of Mr. Snetsinger, some influence had been brought to bear upon the department by some gentlemen who were active partisans in Cornwall and Stormont. Sir. Shields has brought this matter to the attention of tlie government on several occasions. I have a number of letters, but I do not think I should read them to the House, as many of them are marked private. But there is a letter here which is not marked private, written by one of the ministers of the Crown, in which he assures Mr. Shields that the mistake will be rectified. I may say that when I came here I saw the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, who treated me most courteously and listened to the case most attentively. I know that the time of all the ministers is very much occupied, aud that it is impossible for them to discuss these matters at any length. I endeavoured to present the matter in as fair a manner as possible, and the hon. minister then told me that it would receive consideration. That was in the month of February. I have on several occasions since called his attention to this case, which I considered to be one of very great hardship, and I feel that if the hon. ministers had been aware of the circumstances, they never for one moment would have advised the Treasury Board to deprive this man of the superannuation to which he is justly entitled. I

may say that I consulted his physician a short time ago in reference to an accident which Mr. Shields sustained a few months prior to his dismissal, and his physician told me that his certificate is on record in one of the departments here to the effect that this man will never he competent to do any hard manual labour. He received that accident in the discharge of his duties, which were of a very onerous nature. During the winter months he had to get the depth of the water, and in order to do that, I am told that he had to go down a very steep decline, which was constantly covered with ice; and during the winter prior to his dismissal, he slipped and had a very serious fall, the result of which has been that he has not been able to do one day's work since his dismissal in 1897. I say without fear of contradiction that this man Timothy Shields was never an active partisan in any sense of the word, although I do say that if he had been an active partisan, while the department might have seen fit to dismiss him, they should not have deprived him of his superannuation allowance. But I am aware of the fact when L say that he nas never taken an active part in politics. For a lifetime he was a personal friend of the late Dr. Bergin, and I understand that in 1S96 he did support Dr. Bergin, much to the annoyance of those who were opposing Dr. Bergin at that time. I feel that it is only necessary to call the attention of the hou. ministers to this man's case, and they will deal justly with it. I would like to ask the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals now if he is prepared to recommend that the superannuation allowance be granted to Mr. Shields, who is verging on sixty years of age, and who, unless he receives it, will not be able to earn his living ?

I have no complaint to make of the manner in which the hon. gentleman has presented this case to me committee, although there are some important facts which have arisen in connection with it with which he is not familiar. Before mentioning these, however, let me point out to the hon. gentleman that it does not at all follow, because superannuation has not been allowed to Mr. Shields, that the minister has either not recommended it or has declined to favour it. These questions invariably are dealt with by the Treasury Board. This case, if my memory serves me as to the facts, is a somewhat peculiar one. Mr. Shields was in the service of the department, and for reasons of his own chose to withdraw from the service and seek employment elsewhere.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No, not at all. The first intimation Mr. Shields ever received that his services were not required was in April, 1897, when he received this letter, signed Tom S. Rubidge, superintending engineer.

Then I am confusing another case with the one which the hon. gentleman has in his mind. I had one or two conversations with him in a general way, in which I stated, as he has said, that I would be very glad indeed to have the matter reconsidered by the Treasury Board ; but since then we have been so much engrossed with our parliamentary work that it has been impossible to get meetings of the Treasury Board to take up any question about which there is any doubt at all ; so that there has been no occasion since then on which I could have the Treasury Board take this matter up. I have been very much impressed with the facts of the case as presented by the hon. gentleman, and even where there were circumstances existing such as I was attaching to this case, I would still think it was a matter that might very properly be looked into and favourably considered. I am by no means prejudiced against the application, and it will be considered, however it may be dealt with at the earliest opportunity when the Treasury Board is in a position to deal with these matters.

speechtext: I wrote to Mr. J. D. Snetsiuger, ex-member for Cornwall and Stormont, in reference to this matter. He called on me in Ottawa, and said he thought an injustice had been done to Mr. Shields, and would see the minister with reference to the matter. Since then I have received a letter from Mr. Shields to the effect that Mr. Snetsinger had called on him and told him that he had brought the matter to the attention of the Minister of Railways, and hoped it would be put right. I am not asking for any haste in the matter. But, four years have passed since this man was dismissed, and to-day he has no means, and is not able to earn a livelihood. All I ask is, that the Treasury Board should, at its earliest opportunity, take this up and do common justice to this man.

This seems a case of great hardship. A party appointed by order in council twenty-two years ago, paying in to the superannuation fund during all these years, is dismissed, without reason or trial, in April, 1897. His case has been brought again and again before the government, and they have taken no action. The hon. minister tells my hon. friend from Cornwall and Stormont that he is going to get the Treasury Board to reconsider the matter. Has the hon. minister considered that the Treasury Board would have no power to do anything, that having once

acted there is iio power left in the government or Treasury Board or council to reverse their act ? They will require to bring down an amount to this House, and have it voted to that individual. If the facts are as stated by my hon. friend from Cornwall and Stormont, there is no recourse left the government but to put an item in the estimates. Cases of that kind occurred when I was a member of the government, and once the Treasury Board gives a decision it has no power to reverse it. I hope the minister will, when the item of the Cornwall canal comes up, lay on the Table the memorandum on which the council acted, and the order in council.

The matter came before the Treasury Board at my instance, and was disposed of after full consideration. I do not quite agree with the hon. gentleman that the Treasury Board could not reverse its decision. I could well imagine that it would be necessary to ask parliament for a vote in order to cover the time that has already elapsed, but, surely the Treasury Board is not bound to adhere to its decision, if it should afterwards come to the conclusion that the first decision was arrived at in error.

That substantially is correct, so far as our purpose is concerned, but, I did
not say that we had come to any conclusion not to build either end. Some engineering investigations have been made of the Port Hope route, but we have not decided either to accept or reject that route, and the matter is left open in the meantime. speechtext: What is this for ?

This sum is asked for to build a residence for the commissioner at Dawson, and an administrative one to serve for public offices. A building for a court house is now under way in Dawson. No, we are now renting premises for the residence of the commissioner, and at very high prices, too. The building that was erected last year was completed on the 1st of January. It is now occupied as customs house, Crown lands office, registrar's office, and telegraph office, as well as the post office. But this is only a temporary arrangement.

It is to complete the court house which is being erected now, and an administration building, in which the House of Assembly or Council, if you prefer to call it, will be located.

The post office already built has cost, I am informed, in the neighbourhood of $50,000. We intend to erect a court house which will cost about $40,000. Plans have been prepared for a building for the House of Assembly and for public offices which is estimated to cost about $70,000.

the post office and other branches of the service.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WuitKS.

Charleson before the Public Accounts Committee, and we want to get the result of the investigation with the evidence reported to the House before we discuss Mr. W. G. Charleson, but, in connection with this, I want to say a few words in reference to Mr. J. B. Charleson. I find the accounts of Mr. Charleson in the Auditor General's Report at B-59.	I see
that $48,015.19 was drawn by Mr. J. B. Charleson. I find that Mr. Charleson has employed a Mr. Tachd and that be has also employed Mr. J. E. Gobeil. Mr. Gobeil, as I find in the Auditor General's Report for 1897, was employed in the Public Works Hepartment for 3GG days, to the 30th of June, at $2 a day. I understand Mr. Charleson has employed this young man, who is a married man and that he is paying him $2,100 a year. He took him out of the Public Works Department where he was getting $2 a day and gave him $2,100 a year. On the 10th of March, he advanced Mr. Gobeil $1,500, again on the 10th of March, $400, on the 8th of May, $200, on the 11th of May, $100, on the 3rd of June, $200, on the 23rd of June, $100, on the 24th of June, $500; advanced in Ottawa on power of attorney given to Mrs. J. E. Gobeil $50 per month for March, April, May, June and July, $250, making a total of $3,250. Now, Mr. Gobeil's account for that money is in this way. It says amount of account $1,477.24, and I turn to the account and 1 find the first item is preliminary expenses preparing to accompany Mr. Charleson to the Yukon as per account attached $105.50. I turn up the items of that account and here they are :

Gobeil, Dr.

That is the first item in this account of $1,477.24. Now, I want to read these accounts to show how the balance of that was accounted for and taken out of this money that be drew. I bare given you the items for $105.50, and here are the following items :
Cabs, $3.75, expressage, department to depot, house to depot, &c., $9.50; cab to Gatineau and return, $3.50; cabs in city, $3.25; tickets to Vancouver, Mr. Charleson and self, $146; stateroom to Winnipeg, $30; ten second-class tickets to Vancouver, with berths, $690; fare and puil-man to Vancouver (Mr. Gilchen), $93; one second-class ticket (Mr. Champagon), $61; one tourist berth to Winnipeg, $4.50; cars, messengers, packing, &c., $9.25; two meals, dining-car, Charleson and self, $1.50; waiter, 50c.; six meals dining-car-Charleson $2.75, self $3-$5.75 ; leather tags for trunks (Mr. Charleson), $1; telegrams, $3.90; meals, dining-car (Charleson and self),

E.
