That makes a total of $1,474.24 that he puts in on account of this $3,500, and there are three other small accounts, amounting to about $800, and then he credits himself with his salary at $175 a month, making the one account balance the other. I. want to ask the minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) if he is going to take a man out of the Public Works Department who is earning $2 a day and appoint him at a salary of $2,100 a year ; I want to know, in addition to that, if he is going to pay for packing up his household furniture and moving it, paying for his clothes, pay for his knickerbockers, pay for his Stetson hats, and pay for every other luxury for himself and Mr. Charleson. Is that the way the money of the people of this country is to be wasted ? All these items I have quoted I have taken from the public accounts. The Prime Minister promised that he would run the business of this country on economical lines, and I want to know if he thinks it economical to clothe this man, to feed him, to let him travel as the Prime Minister himself should, in a stateroom, and buy a Stetson hat for $6.50, and gloves at $2 a pair. These figures have come before the minister, and have been audited and passed by him, and the money paid out. Let me ask him if all the other expenditures in connection with building this telegraph line are on the same extravagant scale as this ? Later on we will have a good deal to say about the accounts of W. G. Charleson. who sold goods to his father. .T. B. Charleson. for the government. The accounts of Mr. Tach6, who went up
there, are on the same extravagant scale. He not only charges his clothing, but he goes into a barber shop and gets his hair cut and a shave, and he charges it in his bill to the government. When we are pay-iug men large salaries, cannot they buy their own clothing and pay for their own shaving ? It is an outrage to have the money of the people squandered in that way. I could read more details of the same kind from these accounts, but I will not weary the House.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Of course, my hon. friends over there are perfectly satisfied that it is all right, and so they say ' hear, hear.'
What page of the Auditor General's Report?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Y-59. It gives the details of the expenditure of this $48,000. There is one item in this account that struck me as very peculiar, and that is where Mr. Tache charged the government for having his hair cut and a shave, in addition to charging them for his hats and shirts and gloves. Mr. Tachg is an engineer, but Mr. uobeil was working in the department, not even a civil servant, only a temporary drawing $2 a day, and when Mr. Charleson wants him for a special purpose, he gets a salary of $2,100, and all these expenses. He, at least, should have bought- his own shirts and gloves and Stetson hats, and travel as an ordinary passenger would in a pullman car, not hiring a stateroom for himself and Mr. Charleson.

I am not quite sure that the House and the country will be as much horrified as my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) is, and I hope that on reflection the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) will find that he has gone a little too far. What are the facts ? Mr. Charleson was instructed by the Department of Public Works to go into the wilderness to build that telegraph line. The policy of the different departments in the past, and our policy in this case, has been to allow the superior officers to buy clothing which they would not have been obliged to buy if they had stayed here.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Do they not wear shirts here ?

Well, they would use shirts here which would not be quite so rough. However, I think the country will understand very well that when men start for the wilderness they should be allowed some little latitude ; and, whether rightly or wrongly, the department allowed them to buy for their work there certain clothing and other things which they would not have used here. They bougnt two or three shirts for four or five dollars all told. Our surplus will not be eaten up by that amount of money.
What about the silk hat ? Would It be needed in the woods?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: A Stetson hat for $6.50.

I do not know whether that is a silk hat or not. My hon. friend is surprised and scandalized at the fact that Mr. Goheil went there at an increased salary. When he was in the Department of Public Works he was earning $900 a year. He is a stenographer and typewriter : and being a strong and healthy man, Mr. Charleson picked him up in the office to take him with him. and naturally his salary was increased, as were the salaries of all others who went on that expedition. I do not know any officer in the department who would have gone into the wilderness and exposed his life for the same salary that he was getting here. The hon. gentleman believes that Mr. Charleson and Mr. Goheil should not have travelled in a state-room ; hut I believe I can find reasons for it. No doubt Mr. Charleson wished to take advantage of his time in the car to organize his work and prepare his plans, and how could that be done in an open car ? He simply did what any minister or business man would do when he has his secretary with him. The hon. gentleman has read a list of things that were bought by Mr. Charleson and charged to the $3,009 that was advanced to Mr. Goheil to pay the expenses of the people who were going there. In that list he has found three guns. I suppose the hon. gentleman would go there with sticks.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I did not read anything about guns.

If he did not read about guns, I must apologize. However, I think the accounts he has read are vei'y easy to explain. The House, I am sure, understands that when those men went there, they had to be equipped and clothed in a proper way. As I shall have to ask for a pretty large amount of money in the supplementary estimates, it might be better for me to make my statement as to [DOT] the expenditure on the line after the inquiry is completed. Still, I am ready to answer now any question that may be asked me.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: When Mr. Gobeil was hired for $2,100 a year, he was keeping house; and lie makes a charge of $21 for moving furniture, packing, &c., on account of giving up house, and a charge of $24 for storing his furniture.

The deputy minister informs me that he lias struck out that amount. Of course, I cannot be supposed to control these small expenditures. although I am responsible for them : and if that expenditure has been allowed, I do not think it should be allowed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The Auditor General's Report does not show any credit on account Mr. TARTE.
of its having been struck out. Mr. J. B. Charleson approved of the account, and gave him credit on it.
I never claimed J. B. Charleson to be an infallible man. As to the charge for storage, I quite admit that it is wrong. I have not seen It before.

It does seem passing strange that if you take men from the ordinary walks of life and give them employment under the government, they at once become so dignified and important that only the most expensive style of living and travelling is suitable for them. Whether it is a man going to the Yukon or an immigration agent or a civil servant travelling through the country, they seem to be imbued with the idea that they must travel in state. I was going through the country with one of the immigration agents, and a first-class car was not good enough for him; nothing but a Fullmnn car would do. We have expenditures for meals, cabs, tips, and one thing after another, a dollar here and 75 cents or 50 cents there-50 cents as a tip to a waiter. I do not think this is right or that the country will endorse it. I would be sorry to deprive these people of any of the comforts or necessaries of life ; but in looking at many of these accounts, one cannot refrain from the belief that they are extravagant to the greatest degree. Their life insurance is charged to the country. In many cases there are charges for ordinary clothing. I could understand that in going to this severe climate of the Yukon country, a man would have to get many articles of apparel which he would not require down here, and there might be some reason for his charging them, but there can be none for charging silk hats at $6.50, and kid gloves. It looks as if these gentlemen were making extravagant expenditure for the purpose of not returning any of the money and making the account balance up.

There may be something in what my hon. friend has just said. I have found on some occasions that my employees travelled more luxuriously than I did. But in this ease I do not see any ground for serious reproach. The charge is a cow-boy hat, and not a silk hat.
I think there is an increase of $1,100 to Mr. Tachfi. What is that for ?

Mr. Tachfi is a permanent employee of the department, earning $1,700 a year, but when we asked him to go out there we agreed to pay him $1,100 additional per year as long as he stayed there. When he returns, he will go back to his former salary.
I see a reduction in the item for the line from Quesnel to Atlin. Is that nearly completed ?

We expect to complete it by the 1st July next. I have received a telegram from Mr. Charleson, informing me that some of his party had gone over the gap, and that the distance is what he estimated, about 50 miles. The line between Dawson and Ashcroft is 1,896 miles in length. We also have built a line from Dawson to Port Egbert on the American line, 90 miles. When our American friends have completed their line from Cape Nome to Port Egbert, we will be in communication with the whole American system, and expect very good results. So far, on the 650 miles from Dawson to Port Bennett and Atlin, our earnings have reached the amount of $107,000 in the last fifteen months, which gives a clear profit of about $50,000.
What is the charge per message ?

Fifty cents per 100 miles for ten words. Of course we have local rates which my hon. friend will find on page 40 of the Public Works Report, and of these rates nobody has complained. When this line is completed and the branch lines we are building between Fort Fraser and Benson bridge, about 200 miles, and from Fort Simpson to Hazelton, we will have a vast system of telegraph which we hope will be very profitable. Just to show what we have done, we have built about 34 stations and refuge houses from Quesnel to Dawson. I think this line has been built to great advantage. I do not say that everything has been done as we would have done it ourselves; but, taking into account the difficulties of isolation and so on, I think there is not much in the work upon which to base a criticism of the department. I do not claim credit to myself for I was away nearly all the time. Speaking without party bias, I think that Mr. Charleson, who has been very much accused, has done a work that will redound to his credit. He built the line between Bennett and Dawson, 650 miles, in five months, and he has built it well. I do not believe that the expenditure has been exaggerated.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We do not know what it is yet.
There may be some amounts totalling, perhaps, $15,000 or $20,000, that are not settled yet, but we know pretty well where we stand.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) may know, but the House or the country does not know how much money has been spent by Mr. Charleson for the work that he has done. We know only what has appeared in the Auditor General's Report for last year. When we see the Auditor General's next report, a year from now, there may be a revelation.

When the supplementary estimates are under discussion, I shall be glad to give all the information as to the expenditure. I will have careful statements prepared which I will lay on the Table of the House.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I understood the hon. minister to say that Mr. Tachfi was drawing $1,700 ?

When he left-yes. That is what he was drawing as a permanent employee, and we agreed to pay him $1,100 a year additional, or a total of $2,800, while he was out there.
Mr. TAY'LOR. And did the minister agree also to furnish him with board ?
Yes, we agreed that the different officers should be lodged and boarded.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Besides this $2,800 salary?
Yes.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
And did he agree to furnish him such items as this ?
Department of Public Works :
Dr. to J. C. Tache.
Bennett, B.C., March 6, 1899.-Carter to Hull and Gatineau and return, $4; lunch, 50c. March 8 : shirts and boots, $6. March 10 : pocket-book, $2. March 11 : carter, $4. March 15 : valise, $2.50. March 18 : Shirts, $2; hats and caps, $4. March 22 : shirts and collars, $3. March 25 : tobacco, $2; washing, $2. March 31 : snow glass, $3; developing plate, $2.50-
I suppose he was taking snap shots on the way.
-April 3 : two pairs of stockings, $1.50; two felt soles, 50c. April 10 : tobacco, $1.50. April 14 : washing, $2.15. May 2 : washing, $2.60. July 4 : hair cut and shaving, $2.
This is all approved by J. B. Charleson, superintendent of Yukon improvements. The hon. minister not merely raises this man's salary $1,100, but furnishes him with board, and also buys valises for his clothes, pocket-books to carry his money, tobacco, and so on, and pays for his washing and shaving and hair-cutting.
I mav sav that when we increased Mr. Tach6's salary by $1,100, I did not expect he was going to charge us with hair-cutting.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: He charged the country, not the minister.
I mean that. I am very much afraid that Mr. Tache had contracted pretty bad habits under the former government-he is an old employee.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That is the story with everybody that does wrong.

Joking aside, I think some of these items should not have been charged. These, of course, are very small amounts, and it is easily to be understood that the minister cannot control them. There is no doubt something in what the hon. gentleman said -some of these employees when they travel, travel better than their minister. And I am afraid Mr. TachG has done that, for charging hair-cutting is going a little too far. I do not charge my hair-cutting. As to charges for clothing, I am responsible; 1 allowed these officers, who went out there, to charge the rough clothing that they would not have needed here. They have gone further than that, I am afraid. On the whole, perhaps, there is not much to be found fault with.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman would like it, I will read him the whole of these items. There is one account with a total of $640, made up of such items as this, and another of $626, approved by J. B. Charleson, this trusted officer of the hon. minister. And if the money is slipping away In little amounts like that, what is happening in the case of such men as Mr. Rochester, the friend of Mr. Charleson, who had the contract for getting out telegraph poles, and who certifies his own accounts-he and Mr. Charleson together.

I am perfectly prepared to disapprove of what deserves disapproval, but I am not prepared to follow my hon. friend altogether. If Mr. Tach6 has charged a trifle that he should not have charged, he is wrong. But it is not proof that Mr. Oharle-son has acted wrongly. Nothing has been established againsc him.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We have not had a chance.

The hon. gentleman has had every opportunity of proving it if Mr. Charleson has acted wrongly, but he has not done so yet. Of course these small things are inevitable in a large administration. It is out of the question to escape little difficulties of this kind, In the best administered departments accidents like that will happen. My hon. friend has a large business, I understand. Has he not had occasion to scale down accounts that were charged against him ? It happens every day. I go into my son's office, and I find perhaps they have five, six or ten travellers, and they often make charges that should not be made. It happens in every firm.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speechtext: Why say that ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Because they say it, I have seen the accounts. He is the superintendent, and every account passes through

his bauds, and be approves of it. Tne minister says tbe opposition bad every opportunity to investigate tbe accounts. The fact is that on each occasion tbe last two years be lias slipxied away from Ottawa just before tbe meeting. We have this year tbe minister's promise that next year Mr. Charleson will be here, and we intend to bold him to tbe promise; we will have all tbe accounts for tbe past two or three years, and we will have them investigated. But until that time the minister has no right to say that tbe opposition have had every opportunity to investigate J. B. Cliarleson's accounts. We are now investigating W. G. Oharleson's accounts, but J. B. Charleson's we don't intend to touch until next session.

I want to ask whether tbe bon. gentleman is fair or not. .1. B. Charleson has been charged with tbe building of the telegraph line in the Yukon. He started that work two years ago. Last fall when winter began there was a gap of fifty or sixty miles to be built. The Bennett branch had been begun, and plans had been prepared for the Hazelton branch. Now, what would the House have said if, instead of sending Mr. Charleson back to his work, I had kept him here waiting the good pleasure of my hon. friend ? The country would have said that I was a little fool.

Last year when the order went out to Mr. Charleson, he was here, he was seen the next day in the Russell, and the excuse came back that they could not serve him with the notice, although it was left in his department, and he immediately skipped out to the Yukon. The same thing happened this year again, and that looks suspicious.

I was not here last year, but this year I was here, and I say that the hon. member for East Grey would have done what I did myself. That line had to be completed, and I would have acted very foolishly indeed if I had kept Mr. Charleson here There would have been no sense in it. Now as to Mr. Glichen, he is our permanent storekeeper at Bennett. Would it have been reasonable for me to call him down here at this season of the year ? It would not have been possible for him to come except at great inconvenience. The same thing may be said of Mr. Rochester. The hon. gentleman says he has no chance to investigate Mr. Charleson's accounts because Mr. Charleson is away. I think the hon. gentleman would have a still better chance when Mr. Charleson is away, because he would have still greater liberty in investigating his accounts when Mr. Charleson was not here to defend himself. But he will be here next year, because the line will be completed by the beginning of July. I trust we will all meet here again
next year. I do not say that Mr. Charleson may not have made a mistake. I am prepared to say just now that it was a mistake for Mr. Charleson to put his name to accounts for goods sold by his son. I grant that, but there is only one case of goods, only one instance, so far as we have been able to find, in which Mr. Charleson's name is alone. It was a case of wire to which his name alone was attached. The wire has been sent, we will produce the bills of lading. But, Mr. Charleson is guilty of having a son.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That is out of order.

I will not say it again. Mr. Charleson is guilty of having a couple of sons and of loving them. I must remind the committee that these purchases of goods that have been made in Mr. Charleson's store have not always been made by him. They have scarcely ever been made by him. The officers of the Public Works Department have bought at Mr. Charleson's store here more than the old man has done himself. I do not mean to say anything in an offensive way, but there is a kind of free masonry amongst these public employees. They like to encourage each other. They are under no obligation to buy at Charleson's. I do not see why they have bought more there than anywhere else. Mr. Charleson's name was on the patronage list as other names are. Mr. TaehO bought goods there, I suppose because he was going out west, and the old man was out also.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Perhaps there was a rake-off.
A rake-off ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Yes.

If there was any rake-off I want to know it; that is all. If my hon. friend knows it, let him say so, and any one who is guilty will be called to account. I will dismiss any man who has taken a rake-off.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: No, no.

Yes, I shall. If any public employee got any commission I want to know it. His head will come off. The hon. gentleman should not say things of that kind unless he has the proof. Before he produces the proof he has no right to do so.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speechtext: All the vouchers are here now.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We have not been able to get them.
They are all before the Public Accounts Committee now.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We go through the Auditor General's Report, and we cannot examine the accounts in detail, because the Auditor General has not received the vouchers. What is the good of getting accounts unless we get the vouchers V We want Mr. Charleson here to be examined.

The vouchers are before the committee now. What has happened is this : I had a capable chief accountant in the person of Mr. Dionne. He died, and I promoted Mr. Kingston. We did not replace Mr. Kingston. The Auditor General told me, after my return from the other side, that our accountant's branch was not strong enough. We had not enough men there. The business of the Public Works Department has increased vastly. Instead of dealing with $2,000,000, or $2,500,000, we are now dealing with $G,-000,000 or $0,500,000 a year. As far as the accountant's branch is concerned, it is not strong enough, and we could not get all the vouchers in time. We have them all here now. I am sorry that they have come late, but it is nobody's fault.

The line between Bennett and Dawson has been completed for some considerable time, I understand, and I also understand that the line from Atlin to Ques-nelle, and as far as Ashcroft, is also pretty well completed. It would be well for the committee to be in possession of some definite knowledge as to the cost of this line. Will the hon. gentleman be able, later on, to give the committee the cost of the poles, of wire, of side blocks, and of the work of construction, giving each separately ? Perhaps the hon. gentleman could give it now; if not, if he will give it later on it will be very valuable information.

I could not give the details of the expenditure to-night, the cost of wire, and so on, but all that can be found before the Public Accounts Committee, because all the vouchers are there. As to the total cost of the line, I can give that now. I will give the details with pleasure later on.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman a question in regard to what are called river improvements, vdiich Mr. Tachc has under his control, and* for which there is a vote of $40,000. Is that work pretty well completed, and did the hon. gentleman exhaust the vote given last year ?

I want to ask the hon. minister a question about the telegraph Mr. TAYLOR.
business. I understood him to say that the rate was 50 cents for ten words per 100 miles. That would make the cost of a message passing over the line, which is 1,850 miles long, $9 ?

No, I was giving that rate for the Bennett and Dawson line. It will be less than that when the line is completed. What I want to convey is this : We charge that much now, and if the hon. gentleman looks at page 40 of the Public Works Report, he will understand the whole thing. We are charging now 50 cents per 100 miles on the Dawson and Bennett line, which means that a telegram of ten words will cost about $3.75 from Vancouver.
What is the length of that line ?
650 miles. As to the other line, when it is completed, we will have to adopt a special rate, which we have not yet determined.
What is the rate for each additional word above ten words ?
Between Dawson and Bennett it is 15 cents per additional word.

I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Public Works if, when this line is completed, he believes it wall be a financial success. Will it pay the government, or the country, to construct this line from a financial standpoint ? We remember very well that the government, two years ago, undertook the construction of this public work, and that a private corporation, which had taken steps towards the construction of a telegraph line over the same route, was set aside, in fact, pushed aside. I fail to see that the government would have any special object in undertaking this as a. government work, unless it was going to be for the benefit of the country. Why should we set aside a private corporation unless some financial benefit was going to accrue to the country by undertaking it as a public work ? I would like to know, since the work has gone so far. whether the hon. minister believes that a very large profit will accrue to the country from the construction of this work by government money, instead of allowing it to be constructed by private capital.
So far this line has been a very well-paying affair. Up to the 1st of January last our revenue has been $107,712.28. and our expenditure has been $57,415.40, making a total profit of about $50,000.
How much capital invested ?

The cost of that line has been $178,820.33.

If the balance of the line pays as well as this part has done we will have a pretty good investment indeed.

Does the minister expect the balance of the line will pay as well ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS, I expect that the line will pay fairly well, but I would not like to make any prophecy just now.
At what does the minister estimate the total cost of all these telegraph lines ?

The estimated cost is as follows : Bennett to Dawson, G54 miles, $178,820.33 ; Dawson and Fort Egbert, 901 miles, $20,000 ; Ques-nelle line, $401,281 ; Manson Creek branch, $73,000 ; Fort Simpson and Hazleton, $40,000 ; total, about $773,000. I may say here that the average cost of the line built has been about the same as calculated by Mr. Hosmer when he was president and manager of the Canadian Pacific Railway telegraph lines. I have a letter in my possession in which he estimated that the average cost of the line would be $340 a mile and the average cost of our line has been $379.
What is the total mileage ?

The total mileage would be 2,0381 miles. I may add that Mr. Hosmer wrote me a standing offer, if I may call it so, in which he said that the Canadian Pacific Railway would be ready to take up our line and pay us an interest of 4 per cent on the cost of the work. I expect we will do better and I am not prepared to rent the line.
What is the estimated annual cost of the whole line for servants and keeping in repairs and everything else ?

I would not like to pledge myself to any definite figure. Last year we spent $57,000 for 18 months, but I received a telegram a few weeks ago from Mr. Crease, our manager, in which he says he expects to spend about $7,000 less than in the past.
It is, only on 000 miles.
It is on 054 miles and then the 90 miles to Atlin. Of course we will have to spend a good deal more on the whole line, but I cannot pledge myself to any definite figure.
Does that include buildings and equipments, and so on ?
Yes, nearly all the buildings are up. We have 34 stations and refuge houses on the Quesnelle and Atlin line and we have as many as are necessary on the other lines.
I suppose these will be replaced by better and more durable buildings ?
I believe the buildings are fairly good. We do not contemplate erecting any better buildings now.
Under what circumstances did Mr. Hosmer write the letter he referred to ?

Mr. Hosmer was urging us to build the line and he wrote us one letter if not two, but I have one before me in which he gives these figures. I think Mr. Richardson had been sent out by the Canadian Pacific Railway to ascertain the cost of the line, and it was on that information that Mr. Hosmer gave the figures.
Was Mr. Hosmer an intending contractor ?
Oh, no, it is Mr. Charles R. Hosmer, who was manager and president of the Canadian Pacific Railway telegraph lines.

When the government first announced the telegraph tolls that were to be charged, they were considered rather high, but it was said by those who are familiar with the country and its difficulties, that they might be considered very moderate. In view of the fact that the minister has intimated that he had an offer from the Canadian Pacific Railway for the line and that he may contemplate disposing of it in some way, I would like to remind him that in the judgment of a good many people the present charges for telegrams are very high, and that they might be reduced in the near future so that the public could reap the full benefit of the very large expenditure we have made. That view of the case should not be lost sight of. The cost of the line does not appear to be so extravagant, but it does seem to me that no private concern should be allowed to get hold of the line and to maintain the present high charges. If that were done they would have a very good investment.

I would like to understand the opinion of the members on this point. When this line is completed we will have expended about three-quarters of a million dollars. Does the country expect that we should try to make a profit out of it, or only to meet our expenditure. I would like very much to hear the opinion of the House on that point. It is not a party question at all, and I would be very glad to receive any suggestion on that point from hon. members on either side of the House. By charging more we could make a certain amoupt of money ; but if the department is expected to pay only the

working expenses and the cost of repairs, we can charge less.

It seems to me that where lines of this nature must come into competition with investments of private capital, the rates for messages should he sufficient not only to pay the wear and tear and the cost of keeping up the line, but a reasonable interest on the money invested as well. I do not think that would be unreasonable to expect. If these lines did not come, into competition with private capital, I would be disposed to say, make the messages as cheap as possible, so as to pay only the expenses of repairing the line and keeping it up. With wise and economical management, I think a great reduction could be made in the rates.	[DOT]
I feel myself that we have derived a little too much benefit from the last eighteen months' operations.
Yes, I think you have.

Perhaps we were anxious to show good financial results. But I may say we have not received a single complaint of the rates. People out there pay cheerfully. We have not determined at all on the rates we are going to charge when the line is completed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I want to read to the hon. minister a letter which is published in the Auditor General's Report, at page V-341. in which the Auditor General calls attention to the slipshod manner in which these accounts were kept out there in the Yukon. It was written on December 13, 1900, when the Auditor General's Report ought to have been in the printer's hands. It is addressed to the deputy minister, and is as follows:-
Audit Office, Ottawa, Dec. 13, 1900.
Sir,-Let me call your attention to the large amounts of cash received by Mr. J. B. Charle-son in 1898-1900, for which we have not received accounts, namely :-
Public buildings, Yukon district.. $ 4,300 00
Bennett-Dawson telegraph line .. 43,615 39
Quesnel-Atlin telegraph line	 1,000 00
Lewes and Yukon rivers	 47,710 86

In an interview which I had about two weeks ago with yourself and the accountant, Mr. Kingston said that some of these vouchers had reached him, though in an incomplete state; but that he had not then time to examine them (as required by the Audit Act) before transmitting them to this office.
I also understood that you were to ask Mr. Charleson (who had returned to Ottawa) to call at the Audit Office and give whatever information he could; and that you were to telegraph to Vancouver to bring Mr. Hardy, who had acted as Mr. Charleson's accountant. I have seen neither of these gentlemen; please let me know when I may expect them.
As was done under similar circumstances last year, I have sent the manuscript of my report Mr TARTE.
to the Queen's Printer, having entered opposite the above-mentioned advances a reference to ' J. B. Charleson's Expenditure-Account at the end of Public Works Expenditure,' on the chance that the necessary materials will arrive in time to prepare such an account.
I hope that this will be the case, as otherwise I shall be obliged to make the requisite explanations in my report to free me from any share of responsibility for the delay.
I am, sir, your obedient servant,
J. L. McDOUGALL, A.G. The Deputy Minister, Public Works Dept.
Then there is this foot-note :
Note.-Vouchers covering a large portion ef the expenditure between March and October, 1899, were supplied to this office on December 21, 1900.-J. L. McD.
Accounts over a year old had not yet come in ; and where are the accounts since October, 1899 ? They ought to be detailed in the Auditor General's Report.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS, The hon. gentleman knows very well that all those accounts have been brought down.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows nothing of the kind, and the minister does not know. The hon. minister cannot present them either here or in the Public Accounts Committee. There is not a member on this side of the House who has seen them.

All the accounts which the Auditor General has seen are brought down. They were late, of course, and I have given the reasons why they were late. Mr. Charleson was out there, and the accounts could not be sent in the regular way. Mr. Hardy, the' accountant, has been here and has been examined by the Public Accounts Committee, and he has been kept here when he should be out there. I do not see that there is any reason at all for complaint. My hon. friend knows that it is impossible to expect that things will be done as regularly in that part of the country as they are done here in Ottawa. All these accounts are down now.
Telegraph Line-Dawson to Fort Egbert, $8,000.
What is going on with that ?

That line covers 90} miles between Dawson and the American frontier. When the American government shall have completed its line from Cape Nome to Fort Egbert, we shall be in communication with the American system. The Americans could not complete their line last year, because their wires and other supplies were lost on a boat which sank ; but they are building it now. We built that line from Dawson to Port Egbert after communicating with Major General Greeley of the American army, who called our attention to the great advantages for the two countries of having our lines connected together at that place.
When do the Americans expect to have their line from Cape Nome to Egbert completed ?

They had built 15 to 20 miles, when they met with that accident. A barge load of wires and other supplies sank, but they are now working on the line, and expect to complete it this year.
Trail roads and bridges, $40,000.

These are roads from Dawson to different points. Some were built under the control of Mr. Ogilvie, for which we have paid. Many of them have been built under the control of Mr. Tachfi himself, with the consent of the Yukon council. It is most important that we should build more roads as quickly as possible, and I intend asking a large amount in the supplementaries.
Lewes and Yukon rivers improvements, including allowance of $1,100 per annum to superintending engineer J. G. TaehS, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $40,000.
How much work has yet to be done iu the river improvement ?

Mr. Tachd reports that it will be necessary to spend between $30,000 and $40,000 in building improvements on the Lewes and Yukon rivers. Some pretty large works have already been done, and we have received from Major Bond, agent of the underwriters at Montreal, a flattering letter, in which he says that the works are very useful indeed. This will complete the work.
What works other than telegraph lines are under Mr. Charleson ?
Only the telegraph lines. I asked him to look about and see if there was anything he could report, but he is only in charge of the telegraph lines, and has his hands full.
Has there not been some sort of joint control by Mr. Charleson over the river improvements as well as the telegraphs?

When Mr. Charleson first left, we thought it would be better to have all the works under his control, but later we found that, on account of the distances and the different kinds of work, it would be better to divide it up. Mr. Tachg was instructed to supervise the river and lake improvements, and Mr. Charleson was given control of the telegraph lines. Mr. Fuller has control of the public buildings.
How long were the public buildings and river improvements under Mr. Charleson's control ?

Mr. Charleson practically never exercised 135
any control except over the telegraph lines, as it was found impracticable that he could also direct the other services.
From whom does Air. Fuller receive his instructions ?
He receives all his instructions from the department.

I find by the Auditor General's Report that that officer complains that Air. Hardy, though accountant for Mr. Charleson, has given no explanation of the moneys expended by Air. Charleson. I would like to know if the Auditor General has had satisfaction from Air. Hardy with regard to this matter ?

Certainly he has. Air. Hardy was away when the Auditor General wrote. Since then he has come back ar.d has been m Ottawa for four or five months. All the vouchers had been placed in the Auditor General's hands, and Air. Hardy has beeu before the Public Accounts Committee-I believe he is under examination now.

I do not know whether it is proper to refer to the matter, it not being now before the committee, but in connection with Mr. Hardy's evidence it struck me as unbusinesslike that Air. Rochester, who went up to look after the accounts in the interest of the government, at a certain time becomes a sub-contractor under Air. Charleson, yet goes on keeping these accounts in which he himself is interested, as a large share of the money goes to him. But there is nothing to show when Air. Rochester ceased to be a civil servant and became a sub-contractor. The work seems to have been carried on in the most unbusinesslike way, and it was impossible to get a clear and definite understanding of the real relationship between the officer who was employed to spend all this money and this book-keeper who afterwards became a subcontractor.

It may be*a little irregular to refer to this matter, but as my hon. friend (Air. Sproule) has called attention to it, I may explain what happened. Air. Rochester left here as an employee of the Public Works Department. having the position of foreman and book-keeper. He was an experienced man and was chosen by Air. Charleson himself. He opened the books and kept them well. The books are here now and are before the Public Accounts Committee. They have gone throtigh the hands of the Auditor General and are public property. They are very well kept. At a given day, Air. Charleson made a contract with Air. Rochester for poles. Whether is was well or not, whether it was prudent or not, I am not prepared to say, but Air. Charleson gave this contract.



Mr. Rochester agreeing to keep the accounts at night without pay. I got that information from Air. Charleson, for I asked him to explain why he had given this contract to Mr. Rochester. He said that he thought it was beneficial to the department to give him that contract. Air. Hardy swore that Air. Rochester was the only one that could keep the books.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then why did not Air. Charleson keep him at it ?
Whether it was prudent or not to give that contract the future will prove. It has not been shown yet that anything wrong was done.

I can tell the hon. gentleman that the books are far from being well kept. He has never looked through the books, for he is too good an accountant to make such a statement if he had examined them. I do not care to comment on this matter at the present time, but I cannot allow the hon. gentleman to send the statement abroad that the books were well kept. I am not speaking of the general outcome of this work, but simply of the way the books were kept.
The A1INISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. I am not an expert accountant; but I heard Mr. Reid and Air. Hardy, two able men, state under oath that the books were well kept.
No.

Yes. Air. Reid said that things were in good shape. However, that will be looked into later on. If it is shown that there is anything wrong, we will know what to do. But, so far, nothing wrong has been proven. Whether Mr. Charleson acted wisely in giving the contract to one who was an employee under him I do not say. I do not say that I would have done it.
Did he ask the hon. minister's consent before doing it ?

He did not. He could not do it as a matter of fact, for there was no communication. Whether I was right or wrong, I gave Air. Charleson carte blanche. I hope he has not abused my confidence. We were obliged to give him carte blanche, for we could not control him at that distance. We gave' him instructions, as the House has already heard. He may have made some mistakes, but let not hon. gentlemen opposite be too severe. He has acted under difficult circumstances and has accomplished a great work indeed.
I do not wish to be .severe, but when the hon. gentleman says that these books were well kept, I will ask him, if that is the case, why the books do not show at what time the contract given to

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Air. Rochester was entered into, and what date Air. Rochester ceased to be an employee of the government ?
We have all that.
The books do not show it. I listened to the witness before the committee and he could not tell us.
It would be an easy thing to find out.

Does the hon. minister regard it as a proper thing that a man who is keeping books as between the government and Air. Charleson should be at the same time a sub-contractor under Air. Charleson and looking to him for favours or concessions ? And does he think it a proper thing to take Air. Rochester's services in keeping the books for nothing ? If he kept them properly, why should he not be paid for his work ? These two officers seem to work too much into each others hands. If I were a contractor under Air. Charleson and wished to get the best out of him I could in the shape of favours and high prices, and if 1 were keeping the books showing the transactions between Air. Charleson and the government, I should have it in my power, without much difficulty, to make the accounts show very much in his favour and show that everything was done right. On the other hand, I might be getting great favours from the man with whom I am contracting because of the power I have of playing again into his hands when I am keeping the accounts between him and the government.

Mr. Rochester got the contracts for poles, for which he was paid $2 and $2.25. Air. Rochester had no control over the money. He was keeping the books, but he could not steal any money.
Air. "PROULE. WTas it not in Air. Charle-son's power to give him a higher or a lower price for those poles in consideration of his doing something for him ?
No.
He was the only authority up there who could fix the price ?

The price was already fixed. The poles were counted by Mr. Richardson, not by Air. Charleson, and the money was paid to Air. Rochester after the poles were counted. The fact that Air. Rochester was keeping the books could not in any way lead to any dishonesty. The money could not be stolen, even had these men a desire to steal, whieh they had not. Air. Rochester was getting so much per pole. The poles were counted by Air. Richardson, and on the certificate of that counting Mr. Rochester was paid.
Were they counted before they were put up or after ?
I think they were counted before.
I am told there is quite a discrepancy between the count before they were put up and the count after they were put up.

The most objectionable part of the transaction is this : Here is a party who goes out there for the purpose of building a telegraph line. He has absolute disposal of the money, no certificate is required except from himself. The department is not responsible at all for the expenditure ; that is one objection. No certificate from the officers of the department here is required to show that the goods were of a fair price, or that they were required. The certificates even for the goods purchased for the use of this party out in the Yukon pass under the nose of the department in the city of Ottawa. I saw a certificate with my own eyes signed by parties out there, passing the nose of the Public AVorks Department here, where the goods ought to have been certified to. It is suspicious that a hardware store was started in the city of Ottawa about the time this party gets his credit out there. The goods are purchased from the hardware store and pass under the nose of the department here, who ought to be responsible for every expenditure. There ought to be a certificate from the department here as to the necessity of the goods and the value of the goods. They go from here out to British Columbia, and tlfere Mr. Charleson has absolute disposal of this money. There is no officer out there to certify as to the necessity or value of the goods.

There is something true and something which is inaccurate in what the hon. gentleman has said. It is true that the ordinary officers of the department did not certify to a certain quantity of the goods which were purchased here. But, Mr. Charleson was instructed to conduct a special work. We gave him a staff, and on that staff was a young engineer of great ability, Mr. Boyer, an honourable, upright young man, as all his family are. He belongs to one of the best families in Montreal, and I am sure he Is a sterling young man. It is he who certified to nearly all these accounts. 1 trust in him implicitly, he would not steal a cent from anybody. He is an honourable and able young man. who will climb up the hill. Now, that young gentleman has certified to the accounts in nearly every case. The other officer who certified to the accounts is Mr. Tache. My hon. friend knows him well, and his family. He has been employed here for twenty years. He has certified to nearly all the accounts for the goods that have been purchased from Air. Charleson. Air.
TackS and Air. Boyer are the two men who have certified to nearly all these accounts. The only account that has been certified by Mr. J. B. Charleson alone is the account for $2,500 worth of wire. As I have already said, the wire has not been eaten up, it has been placed on poles there. Well, as I said before, the great trouble is that Air. Charleson has a son who has a store here, and that my officers bought a good deal there. But, I must remind the committee that a large amount of the goods purchased at the young man's store were purchased after tenders. Nearly all the wire, for instance, has been supplied after tender. Now, there were only $06,000 spent by Air. Charleson under the circumstances the hon. gentleman has alluded to. All the other expenditure that has been made since has been controlled by Air. Hardy, as well as by Air. Charleson himself. Perhaps we should have started out in the beginning to do as we did later on, perhaps we should have sent Air. Hardy immediately, but we were in a great hurry. Air. Charleson started to go up there, and I say that not one dollar of this $66,000 will be proved to have been expended wrongfully. All the vouchers are down here. One of the ablest men in the department of the Auditor General has gone through all those accounts, and he has stated under oath that everything was all right.
Does the hon. gentleman refer now to Air. Reid ?
I do.

Well, now my hon. friend has gone a long way. I think he is putting Air. Reid in a very awkward position. Air. Reid stated that he was only there a very short time, that he had not time to thoroughly examine the accounts, but that so far as he had examined them he had found them all right. He never made even a report and he did not bring a figure to the department so far as he was able to state in evidence, yet, the hon. gentleman says that an experienced officer of the Auditor General's Department has gone through the accounts and made a very careful examination of them, upon which he has made his statement to the committee. Surely the hon. gentleman will modify his statement.
I am just going to read Mr. Reid's letter.
Never mind Air. Reid's letter: we will take his evidence.

I shall mind it. Air. Reid went through these accounts; he spent a month at them, and he did so at whose instance ? It was Mr. Charleson himself who asked him to do him the favour of going through these accounts. He did so, and he wrote in the books that are public property a certificate

to the effect tlmt lie had examined the accounts and thnt he had found them all right. But, 1 wanted more than that and he wrote me, on the 25th of April of this year what I am going to read :
Auditor General's Office, April 25, 1901.
Sir,-Mr. Hardy, of your department, informs me that you are desirous of having a copy of a certain certificate that I gave Mr. J. B. Char-leson at Bennett in the month of October, 1899, in connection with the expenditure by him in the Yukon territory. On October 24th, 1899, I stopped working at the books and accounts, and entered the following certificate in the ledger
' Examined and found correct. (Sgd.) J. W. Reid.'
This certificate covered all entries up to and including October 11th, 1899. At the same time I gave Mr. Charleson a certificate on a sheet of note paper. Of this certificate I did not keep a copy, but, to the best of my recollection, it was to the effect that I had examined the books of Mr. Charleson and had checked over all the entries, comparing them with the vouchers and books of original entry, that I had checked over the vouchers and pay-lists themselves and found them correct. These are probably not the exact words used, but the meaning was to that effect.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: Since then the accounts that Mr. Reid has examined have been brought down. My hon. friends have had every opportunity, and they will have every opportunity of looking at them. If there is anything wrong let them show it. Since then Mr. Hardy, who kept the accounts of Mr. Charleson, lias been examined. He is the property of the House to-day, if I may say so. So. I think that everything considered, it is rather surprising that more irregularities have not taken place.
Ob.

Yes, it is surprising that men, isolated as they were, have been able to keep such exact account of the large transactions they were carrying on under most difficult circumstances. They were isolated, they could not take advice from anybody, they had to carry on the works, and they had to buy supplies where they could get them. It is most unfair to say that they bought everything from Mr. Charleson. Nearly all the supplies that Mr. Charleson has bought were bought after tenders were asked.
What was tendered for outside of wire ?

The greater part of the provisions were supplied by tender. I quite grant that some were taken in without tender, but later on, tenders were asked. The Messrs. Kelly, of Vancouver, were found to be the lowest tenderers, and they were given the contract under which they are now going on.
Will the hon. gentleman produce these tenders ?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works

speechtext: They are now before the House.
I have never seen them.
Well, there are a lot of vouchers, tenders and papers of all kinds which my hon. friend, with all his courage, 1 am sure, will not go through.

The hon. gentleman, if he will take the course that has been followed on this side of the House, will not come to conclusions. I have not said one word reaching a conclusion from anything I have seen so far. I do not believe the hon. gentleman is justified in stating broadly what he has said. I think it is only fair to all parties concerned not to come to any hasty conclusion, and I have therefore refrained from making any comment so far, but I am afraid the hon. gentleman has gone a long way to give an unreserved certificate of character to Mr. Charleson. The hon. gentleman has gone very much farther perhaps than he is conscious of. I have been listening to him, and I have been quite appalled at the energy of the hon. gentleman who has always the happy manner of turning things in a way, by some sleight of hand, that deceives the sight, and sometimes deceives the senses. If I had not some slight knowledge of the matter, I would feel completely subdued by the statement of the hon. gentleman, but having some slight knowledge that I do not care to discuss now, I must rebel against the hon. gentleman's statement.
I do not believe thnt any dishonest action has been committed. There may have been mistakes. I do not deny that there have been mistakes made. I do not want to go any farther.

The hon. minister answered the questions I put to him by stating that he had certificates. He gave a certificate of character to this Mr. Boyer, an engineer who was up there. I have no knowledge of this young gentleman, but I have no doubt this certificate of character was deserved. Tliei'e are three prerequisites to a certificate-necessity of the goods, reception of them, and price. Mr. Boyer has not certified to the price being correct and fair.
I believe that Mr. Boyer has certified to [DOT]the price of a certain quantity of goods.
Those purchased up there ?
Yes.
Did he certify as 1 to the value being fair ?
Yes, in many cases lie did. Mr. Tachd has done the same thing.
I do not think so. However, we will see again.

Does the hon. gentleman think now that this is a valuable certificate ? The hon. gentleman has been in business a long time, and is perhaps remotely connected with business now. If the hon. gentleman sent a buyer out to buy paper for the very powerful newspaper which the hon. gentleman conducted in the past, and . does now in some sense, would the hon. gentleman consider a certificate from a person, employed by him to look after his business, who, only, to his own knowledge, and in the face of the party from whom he purchased, declared that he sold large quantities of paper at retail prices, a valuable and proper certificate ?
I do not understand the hon. gentleman's question.
I must admit in all frankness that some of these goods should have been bought perhaps at wholesale prices. The custom we followed in this has always been followed by the Department of Public Works.
Then it is a veiy bad one.
It is a bad one and I found it so little worthy of commendation that I have changed it now.
It is a pretty late repentance.

It is never too late to repent. The hon. gentleman will find by looking at the records of the department in the past that the officers on this occasion simply followed the custom which existed. I have changed that. The Department of Public Works will in future have a purchasing agent as all big firms have, and I hope to be able to accomplish a good deal of saving in that way. If my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) is
ever Minister of Public Works or Minister
of Railways and Canals-
Not much chance.

Oh, yes, it will come some of these days. There might be worse men in that position, and when the hon. gentleman is minister he will find that it takes some time before the minister knows his trade very well. The ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Ilaggart) is a clever man and a sound businessman and a man of long experience, and he has been caught badly some times.
I do not say that in any offensive way. On this occasion we have not been caught badly, some of these goods might have been bought at wholesale prices, but it was only a trifle after all compared to the cost of the work. We have spent about three quarters of a million and nearly all the goods have been bought at wholesale prices or by tender. Some of the goods bought from Mr. Charleson might have been bought at reduced prices. I grant that, but it is not a large sum of money. I would be glad of course if they had been bought at wholesale prices. But let the House understand we were in a very great hurry. Everybody was talking Yukon then; everybody thought there were millions within their reach. We started that telegraph line pretty fast and perhaps a few hundred dollars might have been saved. I will go over those accounts with very great care when I have a little more time, but I make bold to say that out of Charleson's accounts my hon. friend will not find there has been an overcharge of $500 in the whole thing.
Oh.

I do not believe there is more than that, but suppose on a large amount of money like three quarters of a million, there might have been an accident, and we might have saved, say $1,000, I hope I will not be hanged for that.
We will let you off.
Men have been hanged for a great deal less.
My hon. friends opposite laugh ; I suppose they believe I have done worse than that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Minister of Public Works says that he followed the system he found in vogue but he cannot possibly verify that statement. He cannot find from the Auditor General's Report or anywhere else that under the Conservative regime the officer of any department established his son in business, went immediately to his son to purchase all his supplies, approved of the accounts himself and paid for them; in one day purchased $4,000 worth of goods.
Not himself, Tachfs did.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

That is the way the money of the people has been squandered by Mr. Charleson of the Public Works Department purchasing from his son. Mr. Charleson

bought a stock for 60 cents on the dollar, established his son in the business and not only the Public Works Department, but every other department of government rushed to him for supplies and paid him retail prices amounting to $47,000 in all last year, a great deal more the year before, and this year probably more. When did the minister change the system; when did the minister appoint a purchasing officer; it is only within the last few days when the revelations came out in the committee and opened the eyes of the people, and when he was probably told by his colleagues that these things would have to stop.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC' WORKS. Let the hou. gentleman allow me to settle my accounts with my colleagues. I can take care of myself and they can take care of themselves. I grant that retail prices have been charged in some cases ; but, in many cases he has charged us less than retail prices. The ex-MInister of Railways says there are three requisites in purchasing goods : first, that they are needed ; second, that they are purchased at a reasonable price ; third, that they have been delivered. These are the facts. Where is the business man who has not paid too much at times for goods ? I know not one who has not made some little mistakes. We have not been overcharged to any great extent.

There is the sworn evidence of the man who made them, that he supplied them at $2.35, and would have supplied them to the government at the same price ; and there is the Auditor General's Report, which shows what Mr. Charleson was paid for them.

The hon. gentleman intends to adopt a different system for the purchase of supplies in the future. Let me give him my advice in the matter. If he would follow the precedent set by the Railway Department when under my control, of not buying a locomotive or a freight car or even a paint brush or a pound of nails, without giving a chance to the whole public to tender, he would save himself much adverse criticism. If he intends adopting a new system, let him adopt that which is in vogue In Great Britain. There they have a book with every article that can be possibly required, entered in it, with the price opposite each, and let him ask the public to tender for these particular articles, as they are required, and state at how much per cent under or over the prices quoted in this book they will sell them at. Otherwise no matter whether the minister purchase below the market price or not, he will always leave himself open to the accusation of favouritism. The country supposed that it had the government completely under control when
parliament passed an Act prescribing that for any articles over a certain amount there should be open competition. Let this be extended to the smallest article. The minister may make some friends by purchasing from them at retail price, but for every one friend he will make ten enemies.

speechtext: Being that we are discussing the subject of railways, with your permission, Mr. Chairman, I desire to offer some few remarks in connection with the Nova Scotia Southern Railway and the extending of that road from New Germany to Halifax by way of connecting the town of Shelburne with the city of Halifax via Caledonia, Fleasant River, New Germany, Foster Settlement and New Ross. It is a well known fact that a subsidy was granted some years ago by the late Conservative government toward the construction of this road-the Nova Scotia Southern-between New Germany and Shelburne, connecting with the Central Railway at New Germany; that a large amount of money has been expended on construction, in labour and material, from New Germany westwards, toward Shelburne, through Ohio, Hemford, Pleasant River, Caledonia and Brookfield, cut stone having been employed for bridges, culverts, and abutments; that a large bridge with cut stone piers from base to top, spanning the La Have river has been built; that the road bed had been well cared for on a solid base over a large portion of the road between New Germany and Caledonia the road has been graded, and the sleepers piled ready to be laid down, awaiting the laying of rails; that a large sum of money, or sums of money are due to workmen, traders and others, as also to those who furnished the sleepers; that the road is thickly settled by a thrifty, intelligent, and industrious people, and the lands for farming purposes of a first-class character-Northern Queen's, part of the constituency my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) represents certainly not excepted-with the country from one end to the other abounding in valuable timber and mineral deposits, with lakes and streams well supplied with fish to attract tourists and sporting men. Last year a request was made by the people of Northern Queen's. Pleasant River, Hamford, Ohio, New Germany, Forter Set-

tlement and New Ross, to have the road extended from New Germany via Foster Settlement and New Ross to Halifax, connecting with Chester Basin, Chester and Hubbart's Cove, with a view to a market for their products, they being deprived of a market owing to the impassible condition of their carriage roads and no money to keep them up, as well as the distance to market too great. They contended that if the railway known as the Nova Scotia Southern or Hervey road, so-called, were built, extending to Halifax, they would find a market either at the western extremity- the Sherburne end-by boat to Boston, or at the eastern extremity or Halifax end, at Halifax by boats to Europe. This argument being so reasonable I had no hesitation in presenting their request to the gov- . ernment last year, and pressing the claim most earnestly, but unfortunately failed to have the government consent to a grant for more than twenty miles, with the usual subsidy of $3,200 per mile, as appeared in estimates last year, which would only carry it from New Germany to New Ross. However, a promise was made to me when the resolution was discussed in the House that it would be continued further at another time, which caused me to feel satisfied.
I have asked my hon. friend the Minister of Railways by letter this session to meet this request this year, that is to grant a subsidy for the unsubsidized portion east of New Germany, so as to cover the entire route from Shelburne to Halifax via New Germany, Foster Settlement and New Ross, connecting with Chester Basin, -Chester and Hubbard's Cove, making it from Halifax to Shelburne by this route an international line, a distance of about 120 miles having a connection by a line of steamers between Shelburne and Boston, thus giving an excellent market as I stated, at either ends for all marketable articles, the farmer, the miner, the mechanic, the manufacturer, the fisherman, or the lumberman may have to sell, as well as the speediest, the safest, the shortest and the best road as an international road from Halifax to Boston, it being calculated to be five hours shorter from Halifax to Boston than by any other route. The advantage in the construction of this road is, that it will cost little for bridging as there are few rivers of any considerable size to cross, and the lands over which the road passes is a sort of plateau requiring few bridges and only small cuttings. By the way, I am instructed to say there will be no charge upon the people of the municipality of Lunenburg, and I think I am safe in saying North Queen's, for right of way, as the owners have expressed a desire to give the lands over which the road will pass free of charge, so different from the experience Lunenburg county has had for right of way, and terminals, of the Central Railway from Lunenburg to the Annapolis county boundary for which the people were taxed most unequally, as well as unjustly.

Now, I am constrained to say that 1 consider the counties of Lunenburg, Queen's and Shelburne are entitled to certain rights, and as well as the government of Canada has extended and still is extending lasting privileges, advantages and benefits in the way of railway facilities to counties in the eastern part of . Nova Scotia, and has made them part of the government system of railways in Canada. I feel I am not asking too much when I solicit on behalf of these counties I have named west of Halifax that they have like privileges extended to them to complete the road as referred to as a government road, under the control and management of the government of Canada from Halifax to Shelburne via Hubbard's Cove, Chester, Chester Basin, New Ross, Foster Settlement, New Germany, Ohio, Pleasant River and Caledonia direct to Shelburne, with communication to Port Midway, Liverpool and Lockeport, feeling that it is due to the people of the respective places through which the proposed railway would pass, locked up as they are at present in those beautiful farming districts for want of a road to get to a market.
In addition to this proposed road being an international one, with a line of steamers from Shelburne to Boston, it will also be a colonization road, as the young men who have in the past from these places been populating the United States for want of employment denied them at home, will be induced to settle on these lands, and make comfortable homes for themselves, and become good citizens as well as developing the various and rich resources of this part of the province to an incalculable degree.
I sincerely hope and trust that the Minister of Railways and the government will consider this matter on its merits, as well as the strong and reasonable arguments adduced by me, and decide favourably, which will be to the great advantage of these poor people who have spent their time, their strength and their means in completing an immense amount of construction work, and providing sleepers awaiting the laying of the rails, for which they are not paid, and thus no longer delay this matter, or keep them in a state of suspense. Let the government quickly, and as a patriotic government should do, mete out to those people the Just measure of their deserts, and submit to the House, this session, a resolution making this a government road, and embracing in the same proposal, an amount sufficient to complete the entire work from Halifax to Shelburne via New Ross and New Germany. By so doing they will take the first step toward making this section of country, with its rich farming lands, minerals, and forest, second to none in any part of this Dominion.
In this connection, I feel, when making this appeal, I have not portrayed this picture in too glowing colours, still I trust sufficiently so, as to induce the Minister of
Railways and the government, to meet the wishes and expectations of this long suffering and oppressed people, and I repeat I hope a l'fcsomuon as referred to. will be submitted to parliament this session, and I will assure hon. gentlemen opposite that it will meet with the hearty approval of members of the Conservative party on this side of the House, without a dissentient voice.
1 again repeat, I hope the Minister of Railways and the government will meet the wishes of the people I have referred to.
Now, with regard to the South Shore Railway, referred to by the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade), in ' Hansard ' of the 22nd of March, I desire to offer a word by way of correction. The hon. gentleman put the following question : ' Does the member for Lunenburg favour the granting of a subsidy for the South Shore Railway?' to which I replied: 'If they will give us the central route, and that also I wiil be greatly pleased.' Now, I find I am reported in ' Hansard ' as having said ' central road.' which I beg to say is an error, as I said ' route,' meaning when I said the 1 central route,' that it should apply to the roads known as the Nova Scotia Southern, or that commonly called the Hervey Road, running through the centre of the country, and extending from New Germany via New Ross to Halifax. .
